#4243. Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought

As the heart gets older, inflammation increases, but scientists have not fully understood where these changes occur or which parts of the organ are most affected. Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) have now uncovered a surprising pattern: Certain regions of the heart appear to be hotspots for aging-related inflammation, offering new clues about how the heart changes over time.

In a study of mouse hearts published in Aging Cell, the researchers discovered that signs of inflammation and tissue scarring were especially concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root. These areas contain immune cells and connective tissue cells whose interactions change with age, potentially affecting the surrounding heart muscle. The findings provide a new picture of cardiac aging and could guide future efforts to understand cardiovascular disease.

"Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue," said study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. "We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don't age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don't age at the same rate either, even within one individual."

Much of the previous research on heart aging has centered on cardiac muscle, particularly the left ventricle. This chamber performs the essential task of pumping blood into the aorta and throughout the body. By studying the heart as a whole, rather than concentrating primarily on its muscle, the JAX team uncovered important changes in other tissues and the ways their cells interact.

"The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine," Rosenthal said. "It turns out they're home to many of the cells we're interested in, and that's where some of the most important aging-related signals were concentrated."

Growing older is the single greatest risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet many of the cellular processes responsible for the heart's decline remain poorly understood. One challenge is that mammalian heart muscle cells have very little ability to regenerate or replace themselves. To investigate what happens as the heart ages, Rosenthal and her colleagues used advanced techniques that allowed them to study thousands of individual cells from young and old mice while also identifying their locations within the heart.

Scientists already know that aging is accompanied by a persistent, low level of inflammation throughout the body. Earlier studies have found similar changes in the heart, including an increase in immune cells that regulate inflammatory activity (macrophages) and cells that produce and maintain connective tissue and contribute to scar formation (fibroblasts).

The new analysis showed that aging macrophages became more active in genes involved in inflammation and changes to tissue structure. Fibroblasts, meanwhile, increasingly displayed molecular characteristics associated with fibrosis (or scarring). Crucially, the researchers went beyond identifying which genes were active. They also mapped the locations of these cells, making it possible to see how different regions of the heart change as they grow older.

This approach revealed that inflammation and fibrosis (or scarring) were not distributed uniformly. Instead, the strongest signals appeared around the heart valves and aortic root. The researchers believe these regions may act as important centers of cardiac aging, where changes in supporting cells could influence the health of nearby heart muscle.

"To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life," Rosenthal said. "What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging."

Surprising Signs of Aging in Young Hearts

Another unexpected discovery challenged assumptions about how scientists identify aging cells. The team examined molecular markers frequently associated with cellular senescence, a state in which cells permanently lose the ability to divide, often because of aging or stress. As senescent cells accumulate, they can contribute to ongoing inflammation, tissue damage, and diseases associated with older age.

Surprisingly, some of these supposedly age-related markers were already present in young mouse hearts. Their presence suggests that the markers alone cannot reliably establish whether a cell has entered senescence, and that their meaning may depend on where they appear and the condition of the surrounding tissue.

"What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren't where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us," Rosenthal said. "That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don't mean a cell is senescent. There's nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart."

The researchers also identified genes that became more active with age and were especially prominent in the same regions. Among them were Ccl8, which helps transmit inflammatory signals, and Cdkn1a (also known as p21), a gene widely used as an indicator of cellular senescence. Their locations provided further evidence that the valves and aortic root may be particularly important areas for understanding how the heart ages.

"We're not talking about single genes. We're talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts," Rosenthal said.

Male and Female Hearts Show Different Aging Patterns

The study uncovered another important distinction: Aging did not produce exactly the same molecular changes in male and female mouse hearts.

In males, aging fibroblasts showed stronger connections to biological processes associated with fibrosis. In females, the corresponding changes were more closely related to pathways involved in heart development and protein production.

Rosenthal noted that these differences may offer clues about cardiovascular aging in humans. Heart disease tends to become more common in women after menopause, while its development in men generally follows a more gradual pattern. The distinct cellular changes observed in male and female mice could help researchers investigate the biological processes behind these differences.

However, the results describe differences in molecular activity, not demonstrated differences in heart function or disease risk. Further research will be needed to determine how these patterns influence cardiovascular health.

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the team compared the mouse results with previously published data from human hearts. Several molecular processes associated with aging, including pathways involved in responding to cellular stress, appeared in both species. This overlap suggests that at least some of the biological changes identified in mice may also be relevant to human heart aging.

"Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process," said study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.

Could These Discoveries Help Protect Aging Hearts?

Although the research does not yet identify a new treatment, it offers scientists a more detailed understanding of where aging-related changes occur and which cells are involved. By revealing these cellular patterns, the findings could help guide future studies aimed at reducing cardiovascular decline, maintaining healthy heart function, and improving health later in life.

Rosenthal's team is now examining whether exercise, diet, and disease alter the interactions between immune cells and connective tissue cells. The researchers hope to distinguish the normal effects of aging from changes that may leave the heart increasingly vulnerable to cardiovascular problems.

The experimental design also helped the team isolate aging itself as a contributing factor. Because the mice lived under the same conditions and received the same diet, the researchers could investigate age-related changes without the additional variation introduced by different environments or eating habits.

"Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the big questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself," said study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. "Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta."

Together, the findings suggest that understanding heart aging requires looking beyond the muscle responsible for pumping blood. The valves, major blood vessels, and supporting cells may play a much larger role than previously recognized. Learning how these structures change and communicate over time could eventually help scientists identify ways to preserve cardiovascular health as people age.

The research received funding from the NIH Common Fund through The Jackson Laboratory Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (JAX-Sen TMC U54 AG079753). Additional support came from JAX's National Cancer Institute-designated Cancer Center (P30 CA034196).

Additional authors from The Jackson Laboratory included Yue Zhao, Antonios Somarakis, Harshpreet Chandok, Juliana Alcoforado Diniz, Ramalakshmi Ramasamy, Gretchen T. Clark, Brian S. White, Paul Robson, Ron Korstanje, and J. Matthew Mahoney. Leon Frommer and Sikander Hayat of RWTH Aachen University also contributed to the study.

#4241. Forget Ganon, This Is What’s Actually Killing Players in Ocarina of Time Remake

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

You'd think that after spending dozens of hours exploring Hyrule, fighting terrifying monsters, and eventually taking on Ganondorf himself, players would have some pretty impressive causes of death in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake.

Well, think again! Thanks to the game's new Zelda Notes companion, we can now see what has been giving players the most trouble, and some of these statistics are honestly hilarious.

Released alongside the remake, Zelda Notes is a feature within the Nintendo Switch app designed to accompany players on their adventures. It offers a real-time map, additional lore, a photo editor, daily activity summaries, and, perhaps most interestingly, personal and global gameplay statistics. And while these numbers are still evolving as more people play, they've already revealed a few amusing details about the community.

According to these global statistics on November 11, Big Skulltulas are currently the most defeated enemies in the game, accounting for 15% of all recorded kills. Stalchild, Tektites, and Keese share second place with 8% each – considering how often these creatures appear while freely exploring Hyrule, those numbers aren't particularly surprising.

The causes of death, however, are a different story! You might expect players to lose most of their hearts against a difficult temple boss or during the final showdown with Ganondorf. Nope – the biggest culprit is actually ReDeads and Gibdos, responsible for 18% of recorded deaths.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake has finally been released, and fans have already discovered several game-breaking glitches.

And honestly, I can't blame anyone for that one! These enemies are already pretty terrifying, but their increased speed in the remake makes encounters with them considerably more dangerous. Getting caught by one can quickly turn into a nightmare, especially if you're not prepared.

The second most common cause of death is more embarrassing, though: fire. Yes, just fire. Not a particularly powerful enemy or a complicated boss encounter, but simply getting burned by environmental hazards. I'm sorry if you contributed to that statistic, but I can't help finding it funny!

You might expect players to lose most of their hearts against a difficult temple boss or during the final showdown with Ganondorf. Nope – the biggest culprit is actually ReDeads and Gibdos, responsible for 18% of recorded deaths.

At least the third most common cause is a little more respectable. Iron Knuckles, which serve as challenging miniboss encounters, have also claimed plenty of victims. Losing a fight against one is certainly easier to forgive than walking into a flame.

The companion's statistics also track what causes damage without necessarily resulting in a Game Over. Environmental traps, including moving hazards found throughout temples, are responsible for 9% of recorded damage, while ReDeads and Gibdos come in second with 7%.

Some of the original's most charming quirks from Zelda: Ocarina of Time didn't make the journey.

Thankfully, not every statistic is quite so grim. The Hookshot is currently the most-used weapon, accounting for 31% of player usage, while the Lens of Truth dominates the magic item category with 40%. That second result isn't particularly shocking, considering how essential the item is for certain sections of the adventure.

Finally, Zelda Notes reveals that most players are taking between 20 and 30 hours to complete Ocarina of Time. That's a pretty reasonable amount of time for such a beloved adventure, although I apparently took things a little more slowly. My own playthrough lasted around 45 hours, so I guess I really wanted to savour every moment in Hyrule!

Either way, these statistics are a fun reminder that even after all these years, Ocarina of Time can still surprise us. And if you're currently playing the remake, maybe keep an eye out for those ReDeads. Ganondorf might be the big bad, but he's clearly not the one you should be worrying about most.

Link has always been known as the silent hero of Hyrule, but the remake appears to have given him a very brief spoken line.

#4240. Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder

A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open new possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms

The discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

Worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling important features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

To investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

The researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

"We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12."

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

The discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

"Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases," says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term."

#4238. Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy

The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties."

Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy."

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator

To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems

The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important."

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.

This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

#4237. The Original GTA 6 Leaker Pleads Guilty Three Days From Release

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Leaks have become their own subculture, drawing both fans and detractors of any given property to catch fresh news weeks before its intended release date. This can create not only an incredibly toxic hype cycle, but also spawn small cults of personality around the leakers themselves. Those following the leaks will often entertain wild demands to keep them coming, as long as the request isn't ridiculous.

One such leak saga began in 2022, when Arion Kurtaj, a hacker from Oxford, England, cracked Grand Theft Auto 6 far before its intended advertising date. Kurtaj is back in the news now, days before GTA6’s release, pleading guilty to all charges brought by Rockstar. Facing an estimated $5 million in damages, Kurtaj might just get the book tossed at him.

Kurtaj was the very first to break all kinds of news surrounding Grand Theft Auto 6, releasing info not only on the source code of the game but also on major narrative focuses. This leak was actually some of the first news we got about Grand Theft Auto 6’s female protagonist, Lucia, a major advertising angle Rockstar was banking on to surprise fans.

Discord is potentially enabling all kinds of couch co-op play, enabling direct control over users' games.

From an anonymous account, Arion demanded a ransom from Rockstar, who entirely stonewalled him. This led to him releasing more and more clips, amassing around an hour of gameplay, alongside chunks of the early source code. Luckily, not enough for any kind of major reverse engineering effort, but just enough to cause Rockstar an even bigger headache.

Rockstar was far from the only target of Kurtaj’s efforts, with previous successful hacks on Uber and various individual scam projects giving him a layer of infamy long before he tried to expose Rockstar’s pet project. In fact, Kurtaj’s hack on Rockstar reportedly happened while he was in a hotel under protective custody.

While under police protection from a number of rival hackers aiming to get back at him, Kurtaj claims to have hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick active on his hotel TV. He then entered Rockstar’s internal Slack message boards to demand repayment, only to be met with silence.

This can create not only an incredibly toxic hype cycle, but also spawn small cults of personality around the leakers themselves

Kurtaj’s guilty plea also saw him accept responsibility for numerous other cyber attacks undertaken by both himself and members of a hacker group he worked with, leaving his individual sentencing for a later date. As it stands, Rockstar seems to want to make a bit of an example of him in order to dissuade any further hacks, both from new faces and those still at large.

These hacks, while centralized on big projects and gathering info to share with the public, are far from victimless crimes. Even ignoring the chaos hacks like Kurtaj’s cause on a corporate scale, various previous hacks throughout the gaming industry have managed to target both players’ and developers’ personal information.

This easily crosses a line from inconvenient to straight-up malicious, forcing teams to take strides to protect themselves and players while throwing production pipelines wholly out of whack. The gaming industry’s hard reliance on tech makes it uniquely susceptible to this kind of cyber attack. Cybersecurity has become a major talking point as such, making any attempt to slow down these leaks.

Even with launch right around the corner, hackers are surely eager to pick apart both the game and Rockstar itself for any kind of post-launch content on the horizon. Whether it's in the form of expansions or the upcoming multiplayer segment of Grand Theft Auto 6, Rockstar can’t rest on their laurels quite yet; as much as they may have earned the break, launch just means a different kind of headache.

With all the info we have from chapter 5, the earliest moments of Deltarune feel like a whole new game. You know what they say about hindsight, after all.

#4236. New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery

A new wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most important stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery. Developed by researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin, the device uses gentle ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, helping people enter REM sleep sooner and spend more time in this restorative stage.

Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time. This allows researchers to influence brain regions involved in sleep while simultaneously tracking how the brain responds.

REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. It also plays an important role in processing emotions, consolidating memories, and adapting to stress. Disturbances in this stage of sleep have been associated with several mental health conditions, making it an important target for new treatments.

"This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," said Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort.

"Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up new possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering. Wang supervised Tang's research and served as the principal investigator (PI) overseeing the project.

Sleep Patch Helps People Reach REM Sleep 43 Minutes Faster

The early results suggest that the technology can make a measurable difference in how people experience REM sleep.

In a study involving 28 participants, published in Nature Communications, people using the patch entered REM sleep an average of 43 minutes sooner and spent approximately 16 additional minutes in that stage.

These improvements were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing certain sleep difficulties. The volunteers also reported that the patch was comfortable to wear, with minimal adverse effects.

Unlike medications that affect the body more broadly, NEUSLeeP is designed to deliver stimulation to specific brain regions involved in sleep regulation. It uses ultrasound, a form of sound energy with frequencies beyond human hearing, to reach areas beneath the surface of the brain without requiring an invasive procedure.

The findings are encouraging, although the relatively small study means that larger trials will be needed to determine how consistently the technology works and whether its benefits persist over time.

Potential Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health

The researchers also found evidence that the patch's effects may extend beyond increasing REM sleep.

Among healthy participants, ultrasound stimulation improved heart rate variability, a measure of the natural differences in time between consecutive heartbeats. This measurement provides insight into how the body's nervous system responds to stress and adjusts to changing conditions.

Brain imaging revealed changes in neural circuits involved in emotional processing. Together, these findings suggest that improving REM sleep through targeted stimulation could potentially support emotional regulation and the ability to cope with stress.

"REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being."

These possibilities are especially interesting because REM sleep disturbances have been linked to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Current approaches to sleep problems often involve medication or behavioral therapy. Although these treatments can be effective, medications may produce unwanted side effects, and existing approaches do not always directly address the biological processes responsible for disrupted REM sleep.

A device capable of influencing those processes without drugs or surgery could therefore offer an additional treatment option. However, the researchers have not yet established whether NEUSLeeP can improve symptoms of mental health disorders.

A New Direction for Treating Insomnia and PTSD

Building on the initial findings, the research team plans to conduct larger clinical trials to confirm the patch's effects and investigate its potential use in people with PTSD, depression, and chronic insomnia.

Beyond treating sleep disorders, the technology could eventually support sleep monitoring at home and provide scientists with a new way to study how deep brain regions influence sleep. Researchers also envision personalized therapies that could be adjusted to individual sleep patterns and needs.

"Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," said Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need."

The team is already taking steps toward making NEUSLeeP available beyond the research setting. Working with the university's commercialization unit, Discovery to Impact, the researchers are exploring how to bring the device to market and have filed a patent application covering the technology.

If future studies confirm the early results, this wearable ultrasound patch could become a valuable new tool for improving REM sleep and potentially addressing conditions associated with poor sleep.

Other members of the research team include William D. Moscoso-Barrera, Mengxia Yu, Mengmeng Yao, Jinmo Jeong, Ilya Pyatnitskiy, Anakaren Romero Lozano, Jiachen Wang, Ju-Chun Hsieh, Tony Sungjin Chae, Daniel Song, Julieta Garcia, Rithvik Mittapalli, and Adam Bush of the Department of Biomedical Engineering; Benjamin Baird of the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Psychology; and Wynn Legon of Virginia Tech's Fralin Biomedical Research Institute.

#4235. Legendary game creator Vince Zampella has passed away

Vince Zampella, co-creator of Call of Duty, and a veteran studio head responsible for some of the biggest franchises in the world, is gone.

Vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died. Zampella, 55, died in a car crash in Los Angeles on Sunday. The fatal crash killed him, along with the occupant of his car.

According to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles. Zampella was unfortunately trapped in an ensuing car fire, and the passenger was ejected.

Vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators. His storied career is long, and is responsible for some of the biggest shooter franchises in history. It started with Medal of Honor in the 90s, a game that changed WW2 shooters forever.

Zampella later co-founded the legendary Infinity Ward in 2002, the team that would go on to redefine multiplayer shooters forever. Infinity Ward is the studio responsible for the Call of Duty series, which remains one of the biggest games for publisher Activision, and the entire industry.

Zampella then left the studio he founded in 2010 following a major fallout with Activision. He, along with longtime collaborator, Jason West, went to rival publisher EA to form Respawn Entertainment.

Respawn went on to create the Titanfall series, and later Apex Legends. The studio is responsible for non-shooters, of course, like the third-person action game series Star Wars Jedi. Zampella was instrumental in making the game possible, having hired God of War 3 director Stig Asmussen to helm a team within Respawn out of a desire to diversify the studio’s output and prove he can do more than make shooters.

Zampella had only recently met with journalists and peers at The Game Awards, where Battlefield 6 was nominated for multiple awards. Battlefield 6 is the most successful game in series history, in part as a result of Zampella’s leadership. The legendary leader was given the reigns of the struggling multiplayer shooter franchise in 2021, with a goal of finding a viable future.

Zampella’s sudden death has shaken the industry, and many mourn his loss as the news started spreading.

“We are heartbroken by the loss of Vince Zampella, a creative leader whose work shaped generations of players and helped define what modern shooters and action games could be,” EA said in a statement.

“While his impact reached far beyond any one game or studio, we will remember Vince for how he showed up every day, trusting his teams, encouraging bold ideas, and believing in Battlefield and the people building it. We are deeply grateful for his leadership, his generosity, and the care he brought to everything he touched, and we will carry that forward with us.”

#4234. Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

Researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the new findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk

To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

People consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

Moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks

The clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

However, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

These percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

"Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen said. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk."

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

Wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen said.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health

To make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several important limitations.

Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

Alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

The researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

Nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an important distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

For now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

#4233. T1 beat Karmine Corp 3-1 to reach sixth straight Worlds semi-final against Bilibili Gaming

T1 are through to the Worlds 2026 semi-finals after ending Karmine Corp's run in four games. Bilibili Gaming now stand between the Korean side and a place in the Brooklyn final.

The quarter-final was played on Friday 6 November at the Credit Union of Texas Event Center in Allen, Texas. The Korean side took the first two games in 36 and 30 minutes. Karmine Corp pulled one back over 37 minutes. T1 then closed out the series in 35 minutes.

The result puts T1 in the Worlds semi-finals for a sixth year running, a streak that began in 2021, Sports Kyunghyang reported. Bilibili Gaming await them on Sunday 8 November, with a place in the final at stake.

Karmine Corp’s tournament began on 15 October. They beat Cloud9 3-2 in the Play-In. In the Swiss Stage, the French organisation opened with a 1-0 win over Anyone’s Legend. Defeats to LYON and Bilibili Gaming followed. Karmine Corp then beat CTBC Flying Oyster 2-0 and Movistar KOI 2-0 to reach the knockouts.

Karmine Corp sat 13th on 1785 in the Elo power rankings, just behind their opponents. The teams had also split their two earlier meetings this year. T1 won 3-0 at the Mid-Season Invitational on 29 June. Karmine Corp won 2-1 at the Esports World Cup on 18 July.

T1 reached the knockouts with wins over LOS, CTBC Flying Oyster and Movistar KOI. Their one Swiss Stage defeat came against Dplus KIA. Bilibili Gaming swept that same Dplus KIA side 3-0 in the first quarter-final on 5 November. In the Swiss Stage, they also beat Hanwha Life Esports 2-0 and Karmine Corp 1-0.

The most recent meeting between the semi-finalists went to Bilibili Gaming. That was a best-of-one in the Esports World Cup 2026 group stage.

The other semi-final is Gen.G against Invictus Gaming on Saturday 7 November at 16:00 Central Time. Gen.G beat LYON 3-0 in their quarter-final. Invictus Gaming beat Top Esports 3-1. Nineteen teams started the tournament, which has a total prize pool of $5,000,000.

#4232. 10 Great Games That Defined The Xbox Series X|S

Eric Warner is a Journalist and Multimedia Producer based in New England with over 7 years of experience producing stories for multiple publications

It’s rare for gaming brands to last through three console generations, let alone four. Microsoft’s gaming brand, Xbox, has managed to do just that, reaching the momentous milestone of creating gaming memories for 25 years.

However, Xbox’s fourth and current console generation, the Xbox Series X|S, has been impacted by an ongoing identity crisis for the brand, with Xbox initially focusing on acquiring studios, Game Pass, and Play Anywhere, only to lay off hundreds of employees and refocus on developing exclusive titles.

Despite that rocky history, there were still many great exclusive and Microsoft-supported games that launched on the Xbox Series X|S and showcased Xbox’s ever-changing priorities.

In 2014, Microsoft acquired Mojang and the greater Minecraft franchise. Since then, Microsoft has been striving to expand the Minecraft franchise through spinoffs like Minecraft: Story Mode, Minecraft Dungeons, and, for the Series consoles, Minecraft Legends.

Developed by Mojang and Blackbird Interactive, Minecraft Legends is a cross between traditional action games and RTS titles, having players acquire resources and mobs like Golems to defend the world against invading Nether forces.

Like many Minecraft spinoffs, Legends’ reception was overall mixed between critics and gamers, but its unique gameplay style goes to show just how much endless potential the Minecraft franchise has beyond its humble survival origins.

The British video game developer Ninja Theory soared into gaming prominence with the release of the ambitious action-adventure game Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice, but that game’s success wound up being a blessing and a curse: NT was acquired by Microsoft shortly thereafter in 2018.

Since then, Microsoft helped fund and publish the MOBA Bleeding Edge as well as Hellblade’s sequel, Senua's Saga: Hellblade II, which followed series protagonist Senua once again as she sets out to free her people from captivity in Iceland during the ninth century.

While Hellblade II would receive critical praise for its story and gameplay just like its predecessor, its success was apparently not enough for Microsoft to continue investing in NT, with the developer now facing closure and a third Hellblade game facing cancellation.

Double Fine is well-known for creating some of the most creative and hilarious games of the 21st century. They also have a long history with Xbox, having released Psychonauts as a timed original Xbox exclusive and Iron Brigade as an Xbox 360 exclusive.

However, Double Fine briefly joined Xbox Game Studios in 2019 to release Psychonauts 2 and its first Series X|S exclusive, Keeper, a very unique adventure game following a living lighthouse as it sets out to help a bird called Twig reunite with its flock.

Despite its rather bizarre, Dr. Seuss-like nature, Keeper wound up being a very fun, visually wondrous, and heartwarming game that every Double Fine fan and Series X|S owner should give a try, even if Double Fine is no longer a part of Xbox Game Studios.

From Project Gotham Racing to Halo: Combat Evolved, these 10 great games defined the original Xbox and set the groundwork for Xbox's future.

Bethesda and Microsoft have often worked together to release some of the best RPGs as timed exclusives on Xbox consoles, such as The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind, but their relationship solidified in 2020 when Microsoft officially acquired ZeniMax Media and its studios including Bethesda.

This led Microsoft to make Bethesda’s first brand-new RPG in years, Starfield, a timed Series X|S exclusive. The game takes place in the early 24th century in Alpha Centauri human colony worlds and sees players join Constellation, the last group of space explorers.

While Starfield turned out to be not as impressive as similar space-based games like No Man’s Sky and The Outer Worlds, it still managed to deliver engaging FPS combat and third-person spaceship piloting, as well as a wide variety of customization options for the Spacefarer, ship, and bases.

In 2023, Microsoft made the record-breaking acquisition of Activision Blizzard for $75.4 billion. Since then, most Activision Blizzard games have been optimized and intended for Series X|S play, with one of Activision's best games released under Microsoft ownership being Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

The fourth and final entry in the 2019 Call of Duty: Modern Warfare reboot series, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 features a campaign split between Captain John Price hunting down Vladimir Makarov and South Korean soldiers fighting a North Korean invasion.

MW4 is easily the best Call of Duty campaign released in years, ending the new MW series in an arguably far better way than the original MW3 and hopefully setting the stage for more great COD campaigns to come in the near future.

Obsidian Entertainment is famous for creating some of the best RPGs ever made, such as Fallout: New Vegas and South Park: The Stick of Truth, but recently they’ve increasingly become known for creating some of the most fun survival multiplayer games, such as Grounded 2.

Set two years after Grounded, Grounded 2 sees the same kids from the first game once again shrink down to the size of insects as they struggle to survive in the public Brookhollow Park, where grass now appears like a vast jungle and spiders are monolithic predators.

Grounded 2 is still in early access, but that doesn’t stop it from being one of the most fun multiplayer games to play on Series X|S consoles, with players being able to explore and craft in over eight distinct biomes on foot or by tamed bug mounts.

The Xbox had a rough start, but it managed to stick the landing in the industry and our hearts with these great games.

As a part of ZeniMax’s acquisition, Microsoft also acquired the Sweden-based MachineGames, famous for developing the new Wolfenstein series of games. In 2024, it released one of the most surprising hits of the current console generation, with Indiana Jones and the Great Circle.

Released as a timed Series X|S exclusive, Indiana Jones and the Great Circle is a primarily first-person adventure game, following the famed archaeologist in between the first and third movies. He sets out to discover the secret behind the global Great Circle before his enemies do.

While Indiana Jones and the Great Circle doesn’t have Harrison Ford reprise his iconic role, it’s easily the best Indiana Jones story to appear since 1989 and is a pure fun, pulp adventure that any fan of Steven Spielberg and George Lucas’ movies will enjoy.

The Xbox One era was a rough time to be a Halo fan, and sadly, the Series X|S era wasn’t much different. Halo Studios, formerly 343 Industries, only released one brand-new Halo game on the platform: Halo Infinite.

The sixth mainline entry in the Halo series, Halo Infinite sees Master Chief attempt to defeat the now tyrannical Cortana on Zeta Halo, only for the Banished from Halo Wars 2 to ambush the UNSC. Master Chief, a Pelican pilot, and a new AI called The Weapon must attempt to defeat the Banished alone.

Infinite may have launched without Forge, campaign co-op, and a lack of several multiplayer modes, but it still wound up featuring a fun multiplayer that aimed to return the series to its more classic roots. An emotional campaign story set in the series' first true open-world setting on Zeta Halo, it's not to be missed.

From PUBG: Battlegrounds to Cuphead, these 10 great games defined the Xbox One and helped entertain players through Xbox's darkest era.

For 44 years, Microsoft has stood as an innovative pioneer in the realm of flight simulation games, through its long-running Microsoft Flight Simulator series. In 2024, Asobo Studio and Microsoft released the most realistic and visually impressive entry yet, with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

A direct follow-up to 2020’s Microsoft Flight Simulator reboot, Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 features much of the same core gameplay as its predecessor, but with a ton of new additions such as an in-depth career mode, dynamic environmental events and wildlife, and a plethora of new aircraft to fly such as airships and gliders.

Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is easily one of the most relaxing and awe-inspiring games to play in the Series X|S era, as people can fly practically any aircraft they want in first or third-person all over the globe. Iconic locations including Zion National Park, Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, Rio de Janeiro, and more are available as awe-inspiring sights.

Without a doubt, the best game that truly defines the Xbox Series X|S era and showcases the power of the console, as well as the potential future of the Xbox brand, is The Coalition's Gears of War: E-Day.

The sixth mainline entry in the Gears of War series and prequel to the first Gears game, Gears of War: E-Day has players once again embody the iconic duo of COG soldiers Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago, as they witness the Locust’s first attack on humanity in the city of Kalona on Emergence Day.

Returning to the franchise’s gritty, more horrifying roots, E-Day is to many Xbox fans the best Gears game since Gears of War 3, as it not only features an epic yet somber campaign but features a highly addictive multiplayer spearheaded by the new PvE mode Horde Siege. Every element of the series at its best.

From Kinect Star Wars to Halo 3, these 10 great games defined the Xbox 360 and the era when Xbox was at the top of the gaming industry.

#4231. Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

"What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an important mental health concern that deserves attention."

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link

The connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

"Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood."

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is important because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

The findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

"Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support."

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an important role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked."

#4230. Death Stranding Isolations Animated Series Gets New Teaser Trailer

A new teaser trailer for Death Stranding Isolations, an upcoming animated series coming exclusively to Disney+ and Hulu next year, premiered during Kojima Productions’ 10th Anniversary Exhibition Beyond the Strand. The series was first announced last year.

Death Stranding Isolations tells an original story in the Death Stranding universe set immediately after the events of the first game. Isolations is created by Japanese animation studio E&H Production (Ninja Kamui, Bullet/Bullet, Magic Knight Rayerath) and directed by Takayuki Sano.  Death Stranding creator Hideo Kojima serves as executive producer.

Today’s teaser video provides the following story synopsis:

The Death Stranding—a catastrophic series of explosions caused when the dead crept into our world and collided with the living.

In the wake of this cataclysm, many were forced to live in absolute isolation—among them, a young girl. Although this lonely existence was forced upon her, she soon grows to prefer solitude, eschewing all opportunities for real human connection and allowing herself to be strung along by fate.

In Death Stranding, legendary game creator Hideo Kojima brought you a haunting vision of a shattered world. Now, that world expands into new frontiers with a brand-new animation series.

Under the guidance of director Takayuki Sano, world-class hand-drawn animations have been brought to life by renowned studio “E&H production” (NINJA KAMUI, BULLET/BULLET, the Magic Knight Rayearth television series).

The story is set in North America immediately after Sam—the protagonist of the game—reconnects the continent by means of the Chiral Network. However, as America is reborn from the ashes, the renewed connections that bind it together bring about new and unforeseen consequences.

In this tumultuous new landscape, there are some who walk a different path to the one chosen by Sam and his Bridges comrades: a wise old man who connects people through a method that defies all reckoning; a female soldier ensnared in a cycle of war and destruction; a boy who seethes with rage at the absurdity of his life...and of course, the girl who chose to sever all ties with the outside world...Fate has other plans for her, however, and chance encounters see her launched headfirst into a world she does not recognize.

Death Stranding Isolations is coming to Disney+ and Hulu in 2027. It’s one of the three planned big-screen adaptations of the series. An animated movie called Death Stranding: Mosquito (working title) is also in the works alongside a live-action Death Stranding film by A24.

For more on Death Stranding, check out our reviews for the first game and its 2025 sequel. You can also read the latest update on Kojima Productions’ upcoming stealth-espionage game, Physint.

#4227. Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

An international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

The technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the new approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants

Parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

For some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

"The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers."

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells

The new technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

"We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces."

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

"The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she says. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain."

The process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice

To investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

"Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an important target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease."

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly important because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

After the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice showed significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," says Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

However, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

One possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

"Nevertheless, we are convinced that the new method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately."

Beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a new way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward new approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

#4226. EA Reportedly Closed BioWare To Invest In Developing Star Wars Battlefront III Instead Of The Next Mass Effect

Electronic Arts shut down the legendary RPG studio BioWare last week, ending development on an untitled fifth Mass Effect game. Since then, we've seen what appears to be a leaked trailer for the game, which suggests it might have been called Mass Effect Universe, and heard a sneak peek at what Grammy-winning composer Austin Wintory was cooking up for the beloved sci-fi RPG series. Over the past week, fans across the internet have tried to piece together how a publisher could decide to shut down a studio as prolific as BioWare, but according to a new Bloomberg report, the answer is Star Wars.

More specifically, Bloomberg writes that, presented with the opportunity to develop Star Wars Battlefront III with Disney, the publisher, which went private last year after a $55 billion acquisition,  chose to invest its money into that instead of BioWare's in-development Mass Effect sequel. The publication writes that EA looked at its portfolio for the coming years and had two massive sci-fi investments it could continue: Star Wars Battlefront III or BioWare's next Mass Effect. Even though Mass Effect was well into development, and even though the Battlefront threequel hasn't even entered development, EA chose to continue with the latter. And so BioWare was shut down, and Mass Effect development ended, though Bloomberg's sources say there are other, less significant reasons the studio was shuttered, too.

Those other factors include the poor reception to 2017's Mass Effect: Andromeda, the failure of Anthem in 2019, and 2024's Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which, despite garnering positive critical reception, apparently missed EA's sales expectations by 50%.

There's also the uncomfortable reality that BioWare made progressive LGBTQIA+ positive games but was a studio within a publisher house now partially owned by the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, a government fund from a country where same-sex activity, including marriage, is criminalized, sometimes punishable by death; these harsh laws extend to other facets of the LGBTQIA+ community. Another investment partner in this acquisition of EA is Affinity Partners, a Miami-based investment firm founded and run by former White House senior advisor Jared Kushner, who is the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, a political figure who imposes laws that discriminate against the LGBTQIA+ community, especially the 1% of Americans who are transgender; Trump has also been known to mock this community in various ways. No official statements say BioWare shut down because of its progressive leanings, but one has to wonder if that was a factor, especially after reports that BioWare scrubbed diversity from demos to avoid negative feedback from EA (thanks, Kotaku).

When BioWare closed last week, only 50 employees remained, all working on the next Mass Effect, after years of layoffs at the studio.

A Mass Effect TV series is still in the works at Amazon, even though EA seems to have hung up Commander Shepard's video game suit for good.
