#4181. Devolver Digital is Running a Giveaway for Anyone Willing to Delete their GTA 6 Preload

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

Devolver Digital has always had something of a reputation amongst game publishers as a wild card, a cheeky band who will take unusual, often silly measures to promote their upcoming games. Said measures can range from creating entire standalone games like Devolverland Expo to hitching a ride on whatever the current trend is in pop culture, and whether or not they work, you have to respect the publisher’s sheer commitment to the bit.

Now, if I asked you, “what’s the biggest buzz in pop culture right now,” the answer would undoubtedly be Grand Theft Auto 6. The game is finally launching in two days after over a decade of development, and everyone who plans on playing has likely had their preloads locked and loaded since they opened up last week. However, here’s the big question: would you be willing to part with all 212 GB of that preload for a chance to win a copy of a pixel art sidescroller?

On the official Devolver Digital X, formerly Twitter account, the publisher announced its latest marketing stunt: an official giveaway contest for its next upcoming title, Volvy’s Adventure: Reslimed, which just so happens to be launching the same day as GTA 6 on November 19. Do you want to win? All you have to do is bin your preload.

With 62 bird species to discover and a wildlife logbook to fill, GTA 6 might turn even the most dedicated criminals into birdwatchers.

As Devolver Digital explains in its X post, it’s offering the chance to win a free copy of Volvy Adventure: Reslimed to anyone who reposts with the hashtag “#MakeRoomForVolvy,” alongside a clip of them deleting their GTA 6 preload from their console. Said clip can either be direct captured footage from the console in question, or just a filmed clip taken with your phone, but either way, that preload has to go bye-bye if you want a chance to win.

A follow-up post notes that Volvy’s Adventure is exclusively launching for PC, so while the filmed clip does need to be of a preload deletion on a console, you will need a PC to actually redeem and play the game through Steam if you win.

That preload has to go bye-bye if you want a chance to win.

Obviously, the contest doesn’t require you to skip playing GTA 6 altogether; you can immediately preload the game again after deleting it, and Devolver won’t care. You just have to show your commitment to the bit, and considering the game’s massive preload has reportedly taken some users several days to download, that’s a bigger commitment for some than others.

Even so, the contest has drawn some interest, with a number of retweeters deleting their preloads in the name of Volvy, though others have apparently already pre-ordered Volvy’s Adventure on Steam and weren’t planning on getting GTA 6 anyway. Life is funny like that sometimes.

The release of Grand Theft Auto 6 isn’t just a product launch, it’s a full-on social phenomenon. Everyone is talking about it, even those completely outside of the gaming culture sphere, and businesses around the world are bracing for large swaths of their employees to spontaneously develop the flu on release day to skip work.

Not dissimilar to Devolver, many other businesses in and out of the gaming industry are looking for their own ways to capitalize on this major pop culture moment. Just today, KFC’s Australian branch announced it would be holding a fake funeral to give people an excuse to call out of work, alongside offering free delivery throughout the country on launch day.

Similarly, DJ Khaled is running a promotion alongside XBOX where he’s signing sick day notes under the guise of “Dr. XBOX,” warning that many people are experiencing a severe “vitamin G deficiency.”

I’m honestly uncertain whether this mass marketing push will slow once GTA 6 actually comes out, or just ramps up further, at least for a month or so afterward.

GTA 6 Twitch drops have leaked ahead of release, as Twitch prepares to offer a range of themed rewards for tuning into the launch celebration.

#4180. One Punch Man The Strongest tier list of the best heroes

In our One Punch Man The Strongest tier list, we will rank all the heroes based on their base stats, abilities, and their usage in the different areas. It's separated into different tiers, with the highest being “S” and the lowest, "D”.

On it, you will find every hero currently available to be summoned and collected in OPM: The Strongest, ranked according to different factors. Each character has a distinctive playstyle, of course, so you can always choose who you like for those reasons if you want, but it might not be the most optimal. If you're a little more into efficiency, you can reference the rankings on our tier list to decide whether you want to invest your scarce resources into a particular hero or not.

If you’re looking for more tier lists for games like this one, feel free to check out our RAID: Shadow Legends champion tier list, Arknights tier list, and Dislyte tier list for the best espers. Can’t see your favourite game? Simply search in the top-right corner to find guides, tier lists, and more for whatever you're playing right now. OPM THE STRONGEST TIER LIST You can summon your favourite heroes using the Recruit system, which uses the familiar gacha system, with every hero having a base rarity and specific role. There's a wide variety of collectable heroes, each with its own set of skills and abilities. Here are all the rarities:

In our One Punch Man The Strongest tier list, we will rank all the heroes by their base stats, abilities, and their usage in the different types of content. Naturally, the SSR heroes will be at the top of the tier list while the R heroes take their place in the bottom tiers.

Do not worry if your favourite hero is not available in our tier list right now. You can expect new heroes to be released over time, and when they are, we will make sure to add them while adjusting the tier list in case any balance changes occur. So, make sure to bookmark this page and revisit it in future.

Without further ado, click on the big blue button to view our tier list for One Punch Man The Strongest!

The heroes included in this tier are some of the strongest available. Both Child Emperor and Carnage Kabuto have the best base stats and godly ultimate abilities, making them even greater than other SSR rarity heroes. You can add these two heroes to your roster without blinking an eye due to their superior stats and usability in any game mode.

Child Emperor has one of the highest damage multipliers on his EX ability that can stun one enemy and applies a stackable buff of Berserk to all allies. In the berserk state, all allies will gain increased damage and HP. Berserk allies will also recover their energy at a faster rate.

Carnage Kabuto, on the other hand, is a great Tank for your team and should be placed on the middle row, 1st column to absorb as much incoming damage as possible. His EX ability lets him reflect a certain percentage of the damage he receives, making him beneficial in extended fights.

The heroes included in the A-tier are still some of the best in One-Punch Man - The Strongest. You can invest your resources without thinking much about it, as they are still some of the best heroes available. They possess excellent base stats along with AoE abilities that are helpful in any mode. Make sure to put heroes, like Terrible Tornado, who is quite squishy, in the back line to avoid excessive damage. Planning the positioning of your heroes goes a long way to winning battles.

Out of the above heroes, Terrible Tornado packs a solid punch with an AoE attack that applies the weaken effect on all enemies if it lands as a critical hit. Amai Mask is one of the best heroes to use if targeting the squishy back-line targets, as his skills specialise in dealing single-targeted damage to enemies in the back row. Golden Ball is more of a mix of both single-target and AoE abilities. He’s essential in combos that require Shattering the bosses due to his EX Skill that requires low energy and can be spammed every round.

In the middle of OPM The Strongest tier list, you might be surprised to see many SSRs. However, they are present in this tier because of their lacklustre abilities and low damage multipliers that make them very average to use. A majority of them are still usable if you’re at a new mid-game stage in your journey. You can choose to invest resources into these heroes depending on your other options and roster requirements.

Tank Top Master could be easily bumped to A tier if his damage multipliers were increased a bit. He can increase the tenacity of all allies and attack enemies in a single targeted column. Subterranean King is an amazing addition to PvE-based team compositions due to his AoE skill that applies a Burn debuff on enemies. Superalloy Blackluster is a great tank that can be placed in the middle of the front row to block incoming damage as he gains damage reduction for a few rounds using his EX skill.

All of the heroes in this tier are sub-par and should be avoided. They have poor abilities that are not worth your investment. You can replace them with stronger heroes from the higher tiers after moving on from the early stages quite easily.

Beast King, in this tier, can be used up to mid-game due to his strong row-targeted damaging skills. He can also inflict the Injury debuff that disrupts the enemy's healing capabilities for a few rounds. Smile Man is also a weird hero that can be used with healers like Doctor Genus. His ability to share received heals with allies is a cool touch. However, his damage output and healing output are just not worth justifying his spot in the team in the later stages.

All of the heroes at the bottom of this tier list are pretty much useless. They have low base stats, weak abilities with low damage multipliers, and synergise with no other heroes. Most of them, like Genos and Hellish Blizzard, are given for free at the start of the game. They can be replaced with better ones after you finish the tutorial or the initial main story chapters. Now that you know all about the best characters, go a step further, and check out a couple of active One Punch Man The Strongest codes that will certainly be of assistance, especially if you're a new player.

#4179. Cover Reveal – Tomb Raider: Legacy Of Atlantis

Game Informer’s next cover story is Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, the upcoming reimagining of the original 1996 Tomb Raider arriving on February 12. Since that game celebrates the franchise’s 30th anniversary this year, we’re doing the same with a double-whammy of Tomb Raider features.

We visited Crystal Dynamics’ office to play Legacy of Atlantis for several hours, including an exclusive tour of the Greece section. For our 12-page cover story, we spoke to key team members at Crystal Dynamics and Flying Wild Hog to learn why it’s tackling Lara Croft’s seminal adventure once again (having already remade the game once in Tomb Raider: Anniversary), how this version of the game differs from previous incarnations and why, discuss the teams' controversial use of AI development tools, and how Legacy of Atlantis plants seeds for the upcoming Tomb Raider: Catalyst.

The issue also includes a six-page retrospective of Tomb Raider’s 30-year history, with insights from Crystal Dynamics. This celebration is reflected in our cover art, designed by Tomb Raider franchise art director Brenoch Adams, which showcases every version of Lara Croft from the Core Design, Legend, Survivor, and current eras.

The December issue also marks the return of our annual (and very large) holiday buyers guide, featuring curated gift suggestions for the gamers in your life ahead of the winter holidays. Furthermore, we’ve created a list of family-friendly games to enjoy with younger relatives during upcoming holiday gatherings. Guest contributor Veerender Singh Jubbal writes about India's emerging game development scene and how its community is helping elevate local titles to an international stage. Ahead of the launch of Ryu Ga Gatoku’s Stranger Than Heaven, executive editor Brian Shea played a new section of the era-spanning Yakuza/Like a Dragon prequel while picking the brains of its lead designers for details on the game’s plot, themes, and time periods. Senior associate editor Wesley LeBlanc shares his glowing impressions of Murals, the colorful, fairy-tale-inspired adventure from Disney Illusion Island developer Dlala Studios, whom he spoke with about the game’s conception.

We also have plenty of previews for upcoming games including Final Fantasy VII Revelation, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV, Muramasa: Revenant Blades, Fate/Extra Record, Tiny Metal 2, Mr. Records, and Eternal Anima. We also have reviews for Gears of War: E-Day, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Control Resonant, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Silent Hill: Downfall, and many more.

#4178. Shigeru Miyamoto To Receive The Inaugural 'Legend Award' At The 30th D.I.C.E. Awards

Award will be presented only once per decade

The Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences (AIAS) has announced that Shigeru Miyamoto, the creator of iconic Nintendo franchises like Super Mario and The Legend of Zelda, will receive the inaugural Legend Award at the upcoming 30th Annual D.I.C.E. Awards ceremony on Thursday, 18th February 2027.

The award, which will only be presented once per decade, 'recognises an industry icon whose enduring vision continues to redefine interactive entertainment'. It's designed to honour creators whose achievements have already earning lasting universal acclaim, while celebrating their 'immeasurable impact and influence'.

Meggan Scavio, President of the AIAS, said the following:

“Shigeru Miyamoto is widely recognized as one of the most respected and impactful figures in the games industry and beyond. We believe he perfectly embodies our inaugural Legend Award through his impact and reach, and we are so humbled and excited to have Mr. Miyamoto accept this award at the 30th anniversary of the D.I.C.E. Awards."

Though his current focus is on the production of movies and theme parks, Miyamoto-san is arguably the most recognisable figure in Nintendo's history, and it's difficult to imagine whether the company would even exist today without his creations.

He most recently appeared during a Pikmin Day Direct presentation, during which he revealed a new demo for Pikmin 4 on Switch 2 along with some Pikmin Bloom updates and the commencement of monthly Hello! Pikmin movies on the Nintendo Today app.

#4177. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Read on below for the 1.1.3.5 change log.

#4175. Late Submissions Dominate Game of the Year Nominees

Scott Baird is a Contributor from the UK with over a decade of video game writing experience.

The Game Awards 2026 is almost here, and the nominees for the coveted Game of the Year prize have been revealed, with most of the entries launching near the end of the year, and one of them isn’t even out yet.

While not as prestigious as the Academy Awards, The Game Awards is the industry’s best way to reward beloved titles, as well as shine a light on games that might not have been played as much, all with a heavy dose of commercials and reveals for upcoming releases.

XBOX is collaborating with DJ Khaled to sign sick notes to get players a day off work to play GTA 6, although the game isn't explicitly mentioned.

The official The Game Awards Twitter/X account has announced the six titles up for nomination for Game of the Year. Curiously, most of the titles that made the shortlist only came out recently, with one that is not available to the general public for another two days.

Here are your six nominees for Game of the Year. #TheGameAwards streaming live on Thursday, December 10.

The six nominees for Game of the Year are 007 First Light by IO Interactive, Control Resonant by Remedy/Annapurna, Grand Theft Auto 6 by Rockstar Games, Phantom Blade Zero by G-Game, Resident Evil Requiem by Capcom, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time by Nintendo. Most of those titles came out very recently, and many players haven't even had a chance to finish them.

Of the six nominees, only two came out in the first half of the year. 007 First Light came out on May 27, and Resident Evil Requiem launched on February 27. Meanwhile, Control Resonant launched in late September, Phantom Blade Zero was released in October, while the others came out in November.

The six nominees for Game of the Year are 007 First Light by IO Interactive, Control Resonant by Remedy/Annapurna, Grand Theft Auto 6 by Rockstar Games, Phantom Blade Zero by G-Game, Resident Evil Requiem by Capcom, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time by Nintendo.

Many fans are surprised that Grand Theft Auto VI is included in the nominations, but that, The Game Awards takes nominations from gaming outlets (including DualShockers), so being available to the general public is not part of the equation.

It’s not unheard of for the Game of the Year award to be dominated by late releases. After all, companies prefer to release titles near the end of the year so they can be purchased for the holiday season. There will certainly be a lot of people who won’t be returning to Vice City or Hyrule until December 25.

Clearly, Geoff Keighley and the people who nominated Grand Theft Auto 6 are confident that it has what it takes to win the Game of the Year award, and, to be fair, it’s a pretty safe bet, based on Rockstar’s history and reputation. The numerous delays for Grand Theft Auto 6 proved that Rockstar and Take-Two wanted to make sure the game was just right before releasing it, and fans are confident it will pay off.

Even if Control Resonant takes a surprise win, Rockstar and Take-Two are the victors, due to the sheer amount of money Grand Theft Auto 6 has brought in so far. The award is nice, but the millions of dollars are a little nicer.

We're not just talking about Grand Theft Auto VI and Ocarina of Time, but up to seven video games that could sweep The Game Awards.

#4174. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

#4172. Heartopia surprise launches on Steam and shockingly, everyone seems to be happy

Heartopia players didn't actually end up having to wait too long to play the game on Steam, which is certainly not what anyone expected.

Heartopia has officially arrived on Steam, only a little over a week after it launched on iOS and Android. When the game’s release date was announced back in December, developer XD said it was pushing back the Steam release without offering any hints about how long the delay was going to be.

While the game can be played on PC through TapTap, the developer’s own emulator, many had been anticipating the Steam launch. So you can imagine that when the free-to-play life sim game surprisingly showed up on Valve’s platform on Saturday, there were a lot of happy people.

Heartopia’s Steam release has, much like mobile launch, been a success. We do know that the game reached the number one spot across app stores in over 50 countries, and though the Steam numbers may not be as record-breaking, everything is looking pretty good.

The game peaked at a decent 28,815 concurrent players (via SteamDB) on Steam one day after it launched, and considering how sticky it has been with the majority of those players so far - and the fact the launch itself was a surprise - there’s every chance those figures will improve over the course of this week as it picks up momentum.

Steam user reviews have similarly been quite positive, with the overall rating currently sitting at Mostly Positive, based on over 1,400 reviews.

You’re still need either a Google, Facebook, or Apple account to log into the game, same as you would on mobile. The Steam version does support cross-play with other platforms, so you’ll be able to play with your friends on mobile.

We’ve been playing a lot of Heartopia ourselves, and have been updating and expanding our guides. If you’re looking to get started, such as with how to add and play with friends, how to regain Energy, and how to unlock home plots, our guides offer the best place to start.

Once you’re past the initial hump, you’ll probably be looking for where to find things like mushrooms, bugs, fish, and birds, so definitely bookmark those, too. If you simply like free stuff, our Heartopia codes page is a must read before playing.

It's not releasing on Switch 2, of course, but that doesn't prevent any crossover content from making it our way. And so, welcome to the closest we'll get to GTA 6 on Switch 2, via NBA 2K27, of all places.

2K has just announced the forthcoming season of 2K27's online The City game mode, which'll feature an official crossover with Rockstar and GTA 6. Season 3 is all about Vice City, with Rockstar's already infamous take on the Miami streets making its way into online hooping sessions.

The season kicks off on 27th November, and includes a new Vice City-inspired Park and a bunch of new clothing and accessory items for your MyPlayer, like Vice City and Los Santos jerseys, and Burger Shot and Cluckin’ Bell Employee Outfits.

Here's a handful of screenshots of the event — none of which come from the Switch 2 version, obviously:

The open 'The City' mode is available in NBA 2K27 on Switch 2 (after the console missed out on the larger space in previous entries), though 2K still hasn't graced the hybrid with crossplay, so expect things to still be very quiet.

2K is marking the occasion with the digital release of the NBA 2K27 Vice City Edition on 27th November. This one features Miami Heat's own Bam Adebayo on the cover, and comes bundled with a handful of extra perks (Season 3 Pro Pass, Vice City T-Shirt, 30 Skill Boosts, and 15 Gatorade Boosts).

So no, we won't be diving into GTA 6 on our Switch 2s any time soon, but hey, this is... something?

#4169. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

#4168. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#4167. Pokémon GO's Duolingo Crossover Gives Language Learners a Shot at Shiny Lucario

Duolingo's green owl already has a reputation for making sure you don't forget your lessons. Now, it's offering Pokémon GO players a different incentive to open the app – a chance at Shiny Lucario.

Redeem a code for free Pikachu Crocs in Pokémon GO. Gengar and Jigglypuff avatar items are available with purchases of the corresponding Crocs.

Pokémon GO and Duolingo have teamed up for Duo's Pokémon Party, a limited-time event that rewards language practice with Pokémon-themed avatar outfits and special Timed Research. You won't get Lucario just for finishing a lesson, but completing lessons on seven different days will earn you a chance to encounter one.

The crossover began on November 17, according to the official Pokémon GO announcement, and you can take part regardless of which Duolingo course you're studying.

First, update Duolingo and join Duo's Pokémon Party in the app. Completing a lesson in any course earns your first reward, with more rewards available for studying on additional days. These include up to four Pokémon-themed suits for your Duolingo avatar. The suits are cosmetic rewards within Duolingo, not outfits for your Pokémon GO trainer. To get something in Pokémon GO itself, you'll need the research code.

The outfits include Poké Ball, Pokémon GO, Chatot, and Pikachu suits, so there's something to collect even if you aren't interested in the Timed Research. There's a catch with those rewards, though – they won't stay in your Duolingo wardrobe forever. Duolingo says the suits will expire on March 31, 2027, meaning you'll lose access to them even if you've already unlocked all four.

For the Pokémon GO reward, you'll need to complete at least one lesson on seven different days. They don't have to be consecutive, but seven lessons in one sitting won't count. Once you've met the requirement, you'll receive a code for the collaboration's Timed Research.

Redeem that code on the Pokémon GO Web Store's redemption page using the account linked to your game. The Timed Research will then become available in Pokémon GO.

You don't have to begin a new language course, either. If you've been working through one already, those lessons count toward the seven-day requirement. The important part is showing up on seven separate days.

The research carries the language-learning idea into Pokémon GO. You'll choose a language for the tasks, which will appear in that language rather than the one you normally use in-game. Professor Willow will offer hints if you get stuck.

Completing the tasks rewards you with XP, Stardust, and encounters with Pikachu, Meowth, Chatot, and Lucario. Each Pokémon comes with a special background and can appear in its Shiny form. A Shiny Lucario isn't guaranteed, of course, but it's a pretty tempting reward for keeping up with your lessons.

A Shiny Lucario isn't guaranteed, of course, but it's a pretty tempting reward for keeping up with your lessons.

There's also a language tag for certain Pokémon caught through the research. Tapping it on their summary page shows their names in different languages. It's a small detail, but at least the partnership brings some language learning into Pokémon GO rather than stopping at a promotional code.

There are three deadlines to remember. You must join Duo's Pokémon Party by December 21, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. local time. After joining, you have until December 29 at 11:59 p.m. local time to complete lessons on seven different days and claim your Duolingo rewards.

You'll also need to finish the Pokémon GO Timed Research and claim its rewards by December 31, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. local time. Redeeming the code alone isn't enough, so don't leave the research until the last minute.

I haven't kept up with my Duolingo lessons lately, but this might finally get me to resume them. Apparently, the chance of a Shiny Lucario is more motivating than another reminder from Duo.

And even if the Shiny hunt doesn't work out, seven days of lessons isn't a huge commitment. Whether I'll manage to keep the habit going after the event is another matter.

It's quite refreshing to be able to make some actual progress in a mobile title without opening my wallet. Thanks, Pokemon GO.

#4164. Arc Raiders finally reveals early 2026 roadmap, but we’re not getting a new map for a while

The first couple of months of 2026 in the world of Arc Raiders look pretty promising, but the big guns are being held back for now.

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

After what felt like an age waiting for the Persona franchise to make its Switch debut, Sega and Atlus are now all-in on the Switch 2. Persona 4 Revival is scheduled to launch on 20th May 2027, while Persona 6 has also been confirmed for the hybrid console.

Atlus is in full marketing mode for Persona 4 Revival, but our pals over at Push Square have reason to believe that the company may be gearing up to properly reveal Persona 6 in the coming weeks.

This comes from Reddit user ronakwya, who notes that Atlus recently updated the official website for Persona 6. Apparently, however, this was the kind of update that allows Atlus to perform significant changes to the website in preparation for a big public reveal.

Ronakwya has also pointed to the gameplay reveal of Persona 4 Revival as a potential hint. Its own website was also updated in a similar manner roughly one month prior to its big reveal at the Xbox Games Showcase in June 2026.

So, which big gaming event is taking place in just less than a month from now..? Yep, The Game Awards 2026.

This all seems incredibly convenient though, and to be honest we're a little sceptical. As pointed out by Push Square, it would make little sense for Atlus to pull attention away from Persona 4 Revival at this stage to host a full reveal for Persona 6.

In our opinion, we could definitely see a similar reveal during the Xbox Games Showcase in 2027 after the release of Revival in May (February for other platforms). We're happy to be wrong, as we're proper itching to see some gameplay from the next mainline entry, but we're not holding our breath.

Updated on November 18th, 2026 - Version: 10.29.0 - Added: Silver Moon Sylpha, Hyakka Moon Streamer Tao, Silver Blader Sylpha, Lovestruck Hyakkaken Tao, Nornagestr, Astrea

If you are eager to check out a complete Valkyrie Connect tier list of all the best characters, then you're in the right place. Today, we are going to delve into it and list all heroes based on their strengths, so you will always know which ones to prioritise upgrading.

In Valkyrie Connect there are hundreds of characters, and if you really want to min-max all the content, then you will need to adapt your picks based on the type of enemy (or enemies) you are facing. It would be impossible to offer a list that is valid for everyone since chances are no two players will have the exact same heroes at their disposal. Therefore, take this information with a grain of salt, and don't despair if you don't have the top characters sitting in the S+ tier. You can always use the characters that match your requirements and are next in line, they will do just fine.

Before you go through the list, note that we have a vast collection of similar articles that include a Battle Cats tier list, T3 Arena tier list, Darkest Dungeon tier list, and a lot of others.  Valkyrie Connect's best characters  Let's make one thing clear - there is not one single character (or even a couple of characters) that could be considered universally 'the best'. There are many heroes that do well in PvE and several that are exceptional in PvP. If you want to clear both, then most of the time you need to upgrade multiple characters. That will take time and is by no means anyone just starting out with only a handful of Valkyries.

Of course, some of the characters (such as Vindicator Gratias) can be SSS tier in both Story Mode and Arena, so you should upgrade those first. But if you don't have them, then you can always make two different parties and use them for whichever content you prefer.

If you're interested in a particular hero, you can search for them by name and you will most definitely find it listed somewhere. If you cannot find the hero you've been looking for, then it probably was not released (yet) or is not in the Global version of the game, which is what this Valkyrie Connect tier list is for.

#4161. 10 Ocarina of Time Remake Moments That Made Me Feel Like a Kid Again

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

Growing up with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time means carrying a very special set of memories with you. I first played this adventure as a kid, when the idea of growing up, taking responsibility, and dealing with the more bittersweet aspects of life (just like Link) felt very different from what it does today.

Back then, I was simply a child exploring Hyrule, discovering secrets, and wondering what would happen next. Now, coming back to this world as an adult, I find myself looking at everything through a completely different lens (of Truth, I suppose!).

But despite seeing this adventure with more mature eyes, there were moments when I completely forgot about everything around me, and, for a few seconds, I wasn't a grown-up playing a remake on a modern console anymore. I was that same kid sitting on the floor of my bedroom, playing Ocarina of Time on a CRT television and getting lost in a world that felt magical. So, let's get a little nostalgic today and revisit the 10 remake moments that made me feel like a kid again.

I dare you not to shed a few tears when you hear the first notes of The Legend of Zelda's iconic main theme – it is that very moment when you finally realize this remake is real, and you're about to embark on a journey that has meant so much to you for so many years.

There's something incredibly powerful about hearing a familiar melody return with a fresh presentation. Suddenly, all those childhood memories come rushing back, and you remember exactly why you fell in love with this series in the first place.

Thankfully, the remake also brings enough improvements and new touches to make the experience feel fresh. It's a wonderful balance between revisiting something familiar and getting excited about discovering it all over again. And we're only at the title screen!

Some games have opening sequences that are simply too good to get old, no matter how many times you replay them. And I feel exactly that way about the introductory hours of Ocarina of Time. Running around Kokiri Forest, learning about this world through the eyes of its young inhabitants, and slowly figuring out what we're supposed to do is still a delight.

There's so much to love about this section: getting those cryptic instructions from Navi, finding the Kokiri Sword and Hylian Shield, and finally making our way into the Great Deku Tree. It does such a wonderful job of introducing the world and making us feel like we're part of this little community before the adventure truly begins.

Honestly, just thinking about it makes me want to grab a bag of snacks, sit on my favorite childhood beanbag, and spend another afternoon exploring the forest. Some things never change, do they?

I think we can all agree that this is a canon event for every Ocarina of Time player: leaving Kokiri Forest and immediately sprinting toward Hyrule Castle, desperately trying to reach it before nightfall. Otherwise, you'll find yourself surrounded by those creepy Stalchildren, and nobody wants that on their first trip through Hyrule Field!

Thankfully, that particular rush isn't quite the same in the remake, giving us a much calmer first experience with the enormous landscape. And while I love that frantic moment from the original, I have to admit that I really needed those few extra seconds to stop and appreciate the view.

Seeing Hyrule Field with this new presentation, taking in the scenery, and realizing just how far the world stretches ahead of us was surprisingly emotional. For once, I wasn't in a hurry to reach the castle. I just wanted to stand there for a little while and enjoy being back.

Some of the original's most charming quirks from Zelda: Ocarina of Time didn't make the journey.

Using the ocarina as a gameplay mechanic has always been one of my favorite things about the original Ocarina of Time. There's something special about learning a melody, remembering its notes, and realizing that you can use music to interact with the world around you.

Still, I had my doubts about whether the remake could recreate that same feeling – and, well, it did! Besides, there’s a new feature that lets us sing or even play an actual musical instrument to trigger a song makes the experience feel even more personal.

It's such a magical way to interact with one of the most iconic elements of the adventure, turning something we usually do with buttons into an actual musical experience, making every familiar melody feel a little more special.

That first moment when Link pulls the Master Sword from its pedestal is unforgettable. After spending so much time as a child, we're suddenly transported seven years into the future, and everything we thought we knew about Hyrule has changed.

But the real shock comes when we walk out of the Temple of Time and see what has happened to Castle Town. The once-bustling streets are now in ruins, the atmosphere is completely different, and the familiar kingdom has become a much darker place.

And seeing all of this with the remake's new visuals gave me chills all over again. For a moment, I felt the rush of running to Kakariko Village to check if everyone was still there – since it literally hit me like the first time.

One of the most enjoyable moments of playing as Adult Link in the original game is finally reclaiming Lon Lon Ranch from the terrible Ingo. After all that trouble, getting reunited with Epona, now fully grown, feels like such a rewarding moment. Playing Epona's Song, challenging Ingo to a race, and finally winning back the ranch is an experience I could never get tired of.

And the remake makes this moment just as magical as I remember it! I won't even tell you how many tears I shed during this sequence, especially when Epona makes that iconic jump over the fence, right above Ingo's head, to escape the ranch. That little moment brought the biggest smile to my face.

Having a horse in a video game was such a cool concept back then, and somehow, it still feels just as cool today. There's something incredibly freeing about riding across Hyrule with Epona by your side, and I don't think I'll ever get tired of it.

Nintendo has expanded one of the original Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most heartbreaking side stories.

The symbolism and challenge behind fighting Dark Link in the middle of the Water Temple already make this encounter memorable. You're facing a mysterious version of yourself in what is the most challenging dungeon in the entire game. But the remake somehow managed to make this already iconic fight even more impressive.

And if you've faced him yourself, you probably know exactly what I'm talking about! Dark Link can actually dodge one of your attacks by jumping onto your Master Sword and balancing himself on the blade. It only lasts a few seconds, but it's such an incredible detail that I couldn't help but stare in disbelief the first time it happened.

It's one of those moments when you're simultaneously nervous and amazed by what you're seeing. You can almost feel the tension through the controller as you try to figure out how to deal with this little menace.

I love pointing out how The Legend of Zelda titles occasionally pretend to be horror experiences, and Ocarina of Time has some particularly memorable examples. The Bottom of the Well is easily one of them, throwing Link into a disturbing underground area filled with fake walls and some of the most unsettling enemies in the game.

And let's not forget the ReDeads and Dead Hand! Seriously, who thought putting those things in a game for children was a good idea? I still remember how uncomfortable I felt exploring this place as a kid, never quite knowing what might be waiting around the next corner.

Returning to the Well with improved visuals didn't make things any less terrifying, either. If anything, seeing all those creepy details in greater clarity made the experience even worse. I was just as scared as I was all those years ago!

Eiji Aonuma and the development team for the Ocarina of Time remake discussed how one of the original's infamous dungeons is being improved.

Boss fights are one of the most memorable parts of any Zelda adventure, and Kotake and Koume are easily among my personal favorites. The twin witches offer a genuinely fun battle, but what makes them so special is how much personality they bring to the encounter. They're not just dangerous enemies, but also absolutely hilarious!

Their constant bickering, especially when they start arguing over which one of them is younger, never fails to make me laugh. It's such a silly little interaction, but it gives the two characters so much charm and makes the entire encounter even more memorable.

And the remake takes things a step further with dedicated cutscenes and voice acting, making the sisters even more entertaining. Their performances are spot on, and I found myself grinning like an idiot every time they started arguing.

Reaching the climax of Ocarina of Time is already an emotional experience, but climbing Ganon's Tower is one of those moments that stays with you forever. And I'll never forget ascending that final staircase before confronting Ganondorf, with the intense organ music gradually growing louder as we approach the villain.

But here's the brilliant detail: Ganondorf is actually the one playing that music! It's such a simple touch, but one that made players lose their minds back in the day, especially talking about a time when games weren't always experimenting with environmental storytelling in this way.

The remake recreates the moment beautifully, preserving all the tension and impact while giving us an even more impressive look at the scene. And then there's Ganondorf himself, and seeing his updated design in all its glory only makes the encounter more intimidating! It's easily one of my favorite interpretations of the King of Evil.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games of all time, but these remakes might be just as meaningful to fans.

#4160. God Of War Laufey Delayed To May

PlayStation first-party developer Santa Monica Studio has delayed its upcoming action game, God of War Laufey, to May. More specifically, the PlayStation 5-exclusive title will now launch on May 20, representing a roughly three-month delay from the original February 16 release date.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen," a statement from the studio reads. "We don't take for granted the trusted place in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans. With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20, 2027. We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey stars Faye, Kratos' deceased wife from his Norse adventures, after she ends up in the mysterious realm known as the Everywhen following her death. There, she will fight monsters and creatures from various mythologies alongside a talking gelatinous cube and a talking sword sash. We'll have to wait a bit longer than expected now to see what her adventure entails.

God of War Laufey will now launch on PS5 next year on May 20. In the meantime, check out this newly revealed weapon, then read about how Amazon's God of War TV series has recast Kratos as Dave Bautista.

#4158. Nioh 3’s generous demo is out now, and your progress carries over to the full game

If you’re looking for a way to check out one of the biggest releases of early 2026, Team Ninja has made it easy for you.

Nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously announced demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty new for the series, which has typically launched first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

The Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Another big reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

The demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

This time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.
