#4157. Zelda Ocarina Remake Producers Talk Changing And Maintaining The Game, Easter Eggs, The Bombchu Bowling Alley Operator, And More

Today marks the release of the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2. You can read my full, positive review here. Ahead of the game’s release, but after having played the game to completion (well… 99% as you will learn below), I traveled to New York to speak with Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma (whose work on the original Ocarina of Time marked his first involvement with the series) and Ocarina of Time remake producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi (director of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom among other Zelda titles).

Topics include how the team approached remaking Ocarina of Time, what needed changing and what needed to stay the same, their thoughts on the Easter Eggs from the original game, the fate and marital status of the Bombchu Bowling girl, and more.

The discussion covers a fairly faithful remake of Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64, which launched nearly 30 years ago, but I have spoiler-marked certain questions and answers that might be considered sensitive if you want to maintain surprise when playing the remake yourself.

Mr. Fujibayashi, what is your relationship to Ocarina of Time?

Fujibayashi: Regarding the original Ocarina of Time, at the time I was working for a different company, so it was mainly me as an end user trying to looking forward to the experience of what a 3D Zelda is going to look like. So, really, I was just waiting in anticipation for that.

How long has the remake been in development?

Aonuma: It's actually kind of hard to say exactly when development began because the earliest thought process was us thinking about the 40th anniversary of The Legend of Zelda approaching, and so we started to have this conversation, “Oh, what should we make to mark this occasion?” And then at that point, we decided on Ocarina of Time, and so a lot of time elapsed from the beginning of that conversation about the anniversary until we got to Ocarina. So it's hard to pinpoint exactly when the development itself began.

Was this a more relaxing game to develop after making Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom back-to-back?

Aonuma: Was it relaxing? That's kind of a hard question to ask. I would say it's more a different style of development. So, if we looked at Tears of the Kingdom, Breath of the Wild, these were created as new games with a very different kind of development cycle. Whereas for a remake like this one, we decided to take an interesting approach, which is to bring in this new younger staff and find out what they would bring to this project in terms of their own experience, their own interpretation as newer staff.

And so my role here was really advising them on this, and it's not always like the development cycle of a new game. But in one sense, the producer has to be careful not to advise too much, to say that you must do it like this. You don't want to prescribe the approach that anyone is going to take. You want to make sure that there's enough space for these younger staff members to have their own interpretation, their own approach to it.

Do you have remake philosophies or rules, like what needs to stay the same and what should change?

Fujibayashi: So, in fact, there were pretty clear kind of rules or guidelines, as you said. First, is because you know, as Mr. Aonuma had mentioned, where he wanted to, the development team was centered around the young directors that took part in this development. And when we first started discussing what kind of game and what kind of approach you wanted to take. One thing that really came through and we clarified was, as you mentioned, what are we going to change and what are we going to keep the same.

And I'll start with what we wanted to change, and that was really to make sure that – because we have the ability to use the latest technology through the Nintendo Switch 2 – there's a lot we can change and improve upon, such as you know obviously things like controls, graphics. We also have a new controller, so that allows for the new camera controls. And we’re really able to fine tune and polish the feel of the game and there was excitement for all the ways of expression we can provide the player.

But on the other hand, thinking about what we didn't want to change, we were thinking about the creators of the original Ocarina of Time, and what they wanted to convey, the experience that they wanted to provide for users and players through this title. That's something that we wanted to keep intact and that spirit to carry across. And we wanted to make sure that this new game is able to deliver that in the way that we wanted them to.

Aonuma: So speaking as someone who worked on the original Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64, you always have those moments looking back of, “Oh, you know, I really wanted to do more of this,” or, “I wanted to be able to express this in a different way,” but you're faced with certainly the tech limitations of the time. And I went on from Ocarina of Time to work on other Zelda franchise titles, as well. And with each new title, you're always looking for a new way to express something that may not have been available to you previously. But you always have to keep in mind is what makes a Zelda game special, and how do we protect that? How do we keep that in store for the players, as well. So, on this project in particular, I had to think of that through the lens of how do we protect the things that make it the Zelda Ocarina experience, but also how do I give the freedom to the staff to find their own expression of these ideas? And I think between those two things, we found a really good balance. So I'm very happy about that.

When we interviewed you, Mr. Aonuma, for Game Informer’s Breath of the Wild cover story, Shigeru Miyamoto was present, and he made a joke about the challenge of the water temple. Are you happy with where the Water Temple is now in the remake?

Aonuma: Certainly, looking back on the challenge level of the Water Temple, I think it was hard, but some of that came from the system that we were presenting to players. So, for example, if you look at the way that players used to have to switch to the heavy iron boots so that they could sink in the water, you had to go to a different screen and press the button. But now that we're able to give players a shortcut, single button on the gameplay screen, I think they can get to that more quickly. It's a better experience because they can focus on solving the puzzle rather than having to navigate menus and thinking about that and interrupting the flow of their thought each time.

Another consideration compared to the original is that you couldn't move the camera angle in the original game, and so if you were looking for a certain room in this 3D space relative to where you are now, it was much more difficult to orient yourself and think about the space where that room might exist. So I think those two together, you know, also with the heavy boots being one button press, I think this, for me, is the best version of the Water Temple.

Is the canon of the Zelda timeline considered at all during development? Did you think about adding in Easter eggs that made references to things that would have happened later in the Zelda story? Like Wind Waker taking place after Ocarina of Time, for example.

Aonuma: It's funny because the staff would sometimes ask me about the possibility of including nods to the timeline or references to the other game, and I actually, at the time, would say, "No, let's focus on this game. Let's make this the best version of Ocarina of Time that we can." So, the timeline was in the back of our mind, but we didn't consider taking an approach to this game where we actually, explicitly included references like that.

When testing the game, was it challenging to find people who had never played Ocarina of Time?

Aonuma: As it turns out, both on our staff and in the testing teams, there's a lot of young people, and many of them had never played the original. So it wasn't a challenge to find them.

Who do you primarily consider this remake to be for? New people who have never played Ocarina? Or fans like myself who consider it to be, frankly, their favorite game. Who is the important audience?

Fujibayashi: The answer is both. Our response to those fans who have fond memories of this title is really what I mentioned earlier: being able to provide the experience of what it was like to play Ocarina of Time back to them, and that was our response to them. And when it comes to the players that are experiencing this for the first time, whether it's the graphics, or the controls, or the ability to shift and move the camera; those are all changes and fine-tuning that we've made to make sure that people who are used to modern gaming are able to enter this experience with as little friction as possible. So again, to answer your question? It's really both.

Aonuma: Certainly, when you look at the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, there is so much hidden in the world that people spend a lot of time looking for things. And your first time playing through, you may not find all of it in one go. People in that kind of situation would refer to strategy books and information that they can find.

For example, when you're looking for the like last Skulltala and you already have 99, our job is to think about how to give the player an approach to that sort of a problem. What kind of information can we give them to help out. To make it a fun, but still challenging experience, because we want even new players to come in and to be able to fully experience this world that we've created for them, even though old fans are going to come in with a little bit of an advantage in the form of a lot of prior game knowledge.

I'm not kidding about needing some help with that final Skulltala. I'm going to hand you my Switch 2 after this so you can show me where it is because it's been driving me crazy. I've been having dreams about where the final Skulltala might be.

The end of the game in the remake made me emotional in a way I wasn't expecting. It made me cry, just the whole ending of the experience overall. Were you expecting that kind of reaction from players?

Fujibayashi: So first, I want to say I'm very, very happy and excited to hear you say that because, as you mentioned, that cutscene – cutscenes in general – but that cutscene specifically is something that we, as a dev team, heavily discussed. Because of the limitations of the technology back in the day, there might have been things that we weren't able to convey fully, whether it's because of the tempo of the game… whatever it is. And so, when we approached this remake, we wanted to make sure that we captured that moment in the way that we wanted to express it. So that the right kinds of emotions are evoked, and that we can convey the emotion and the story that we wanted to at that moment. And now that hearing you say that and kind of having that reaction really struck a chord? I'm really relieved to hear that because that's exactly what we wanted to do.

The ReDeads, the Shadow Temple, the Dead Hand miniboss, Wall Masters – these enemies traumatized a whole generation of kids. I'm curious if that was always the intention and how did you approach making sure that those elements still remained scary? Was there a line that was too scary?

Aonuma: Certainly, at the time, we had this intent to make sure that we allow the players to find the enemies a little bit scary. They have to be, right? We want to express that sort of thing. But more than anything, they are part of this Fantasy world, which has both light and dark portions, and so we're trying to bring that feeling across. It’s not that we're trying to scare people outright as the entire intent, but rather show that you know Link is part of a brighter part of the world where people are friendly, and Ganon is a part of the darker part of the world where there's a lot of scary things. And we kept that in mind in the remake as well.

We wanted to make sure we were bringing that out, but the tools that we have available to us now for expression are so capable that if we really tried, of course, we could make something that was very, very scary. But this is supposed to be for all kinds of players. We didn't want to hit the scary notes so strongly that we were putting off new players or younger players, and so we want to have that tuning very carefully in mind as we're making those adjustments in terms of presenting that final expression in the game.

I shudder to visualize what the scarier versions of the ReDeads might look like.

Aonuma: What was your experience of them this time?

Oh, terrifying! That noise. The noise they make. That scream. I feel it in my chest. It just recalls that scariness of my childhood in a way that I admit is very entertaining, and I like. Do you remember recording that sound effect? How did you do that? Did you have someone scream?

For the remake, a lot has been rewritten. The meaning hasn't been changed dramatically, but pretty much everything has been rewritten. What was the goal with the rewriting overall?

Fujibayashi: Yes, it's as you said. We did a lot of rewriting of the text. When it comes to the original Ocarina of Time, there's the idea that because it was 28 years ago – it's a long time ago – there's the turn of phrase, or the way it's been written, is sometimes not clear or doesn't work in the modern day, given the context of the modern day. And so that's why we wanted to make sure that it makes sense and it's easier to understand for people who are familiar with playing modern games, and also that it works better here.

And when you think about… obviously the graphics have been improved significantly. Before we had to do things like… “That blue ocarina that is the size that you could fit on a hand,” something like that, to make sure that the idea gets across to the player. But now, because the graphics are improved, it's very clear what the size it is. It's very clear that it's a blue ocarina. So with the new graphics, if you go through the wordy explanation of what it is, the player is going to be like, "Yeah, I can see it." So in order to make sure that we remove those kind of slight hurdles and really make sure that we can present the game and improve not only the expression but also the pacing of the game? That's something that we really took into consideration as we were rewriting the game.

I wanted to ask about some specific changes for the remake. You get five bottles now. Why?

Aonuma: Because bottles are so important to the way the player plays the game, like looking for strategies to deal with different kinds of situations, even at the time of development of the original title, I thought, “Oh, you know, I could do with even just one more bottle.” I think certainly when you collect all four in the original, you feel great about that at time. But I was still thinking like one more would be okay, right?

So, all this time that was in the back of my mind. But when the new younger staff were familiarizing themselves with the old game and thinking about what they might want to change in this version, one thing that I suggested was that the player could get their first bottle earlier, and this would actually be really useful in terms of reinforcing for the player how helpful bottles were and motivating them on their quest to find the next bottle. It strengthens that whole sequence through the game by changing the order just a little bit there. But yeah, certainly, once you have a certain number of bottles, you're going to feel a little bit more confident and more comfortable. But reinforcing that feeling early on, I think, was important for us in the development of this one.

In the original, there were Nintendo character portraits in Zelda's courtyard of Mario, Yoshi, and more, but those have been removed. I was curious as to why.

Aonuma: Certainly, at the time, when we put those there, I don't think anybody thought it was too big a deal. Maybe there was a more carefree or comfortable approach to that sort of thing. But looking at it now, like if a player is coming through that area, and given the overall way that we're, you know, creating this world and giving the player that form of expression, if they look up and they think, "Why is Yoshi there?” We don't want that moment to interrupt their experience of the world in that way. So we're feeling a little bit differently about it this time.

However, you will remember that there is one design element on Talon with Bowser on it, and that's part of the original design of the character. So we didn't change that. That stays as is.

I have some short-answer questions. The woman who runs the Bombchu Bowling game. What happened to her after seven years. And is she single?

Aonuma: That's something we're not going to touch, and I'll leave it to your imagination.

One of the Skulltala rewards is Bombchus, which I found disappointing when I was young, and I found disappointing as an adult. Why does he give you Bombchus?

Aonuma: So that feeling you had when you got, as a reward for a certain number of Skulltalas, the Bombchus, and you thought, “Wait, that's it?” That's also part of the original experience of the 64 version. So there, there's an approach that we take where we try to keep all of the different notes that people felt in the original game in place. You know, sometimes it's really remarkable, fun things, and other times it's slight moments of disappointment. Even that could be memorable in that way. It's important to maintain that.

The Great Fairies. What do they need rupees for?

Fujibayashi: You know, it's really about a feeling. It's like in Japan sometimes, like donations to a temple or something similar like that. It's to express your reverence for the great fairies.

The 3DS remake had Skyward Sword art hidden in a couple of places, but you removed it for this remake. You didn't want to keep the Skyward Sword art?

Aonuma: [Laughs] I do remember at the time the designers on the 3DS version were really interested in placing Easter Eggs like that throughout the game, and the timing of the release of Skyward Sword was such that it was perfect to go ahead and include that. So I said, “Okay, sure.” But like earlier when we were talking about in the courtyard sequence with the Yoshi portrait. You know, you don't want to interrupt the player's experience by seeing something that's unrelated to what they're currently doing in the game. So for that reason, we decided not to go that way.

Mr. Fujibayashi, you directed Skyward Sword. Were you sad to see that reference removed?

Fujibayashi: [Laughs] No, it’s really as Mr. Aonuma said. There was an underlying concept in what we were going for, so no hard feelings there.

I think the biggest cutscene change in the game is when Link transitions from child to adult. It is now a much more involved sequence. Why did that scene need such a drastic change?

Aonuma: So I think that's really connected to the way we were thinking about expressing things in the original. We couldn't do everything. We couldn't express everything that we'd like to, and I think in that moment where you have Ganondorf having this reaction to Link becoming older, that cutscene in the original, it was very low on explanation.

So, you have these thoughts in the player's mind like, “Oh wait, why is he there? What's the relation to this process?” So, you want something that explains his presence, that explains his reaction to make a bigger impression on the player overall, and that's something that you can use to connect the motivation to want to face Ganondorf in the final fight. Something that I think comes across better now.

[I pulled out my Switch 2 and showed them how I was missing one Skulltala in Hyrule Field]

You can see here I have 99 out of 100 and am have two out of three in Hyrule Field. Can you point to a general location to give me an idea of where to look?

#4156. Quantic Dream addresses toxicity, tech bugs and tutorials for Spellcasters Chronicles closed beta 2 - here's how to get a key

Here are the start and end times for the second Spellcasters Chronicles closed beta, as well as what's new in this latest test.

Quantic Dream has opened up its upcoming fantasy MOBA for a second closed beta weekend starting from today, January 29, until 9AM UTC on Monday February 2.

The closed beta is for PC only in Europe, Asia and North America and potential players can register to join the waitlist for a key at the game’s official website or on the Spellcasters Chronicles Steam page. Players who had access to the first closed beta will automatically have access to the second, but you can sign up on both the site and Steam to increase your chances of entry.

The MOBA genre is competitive in every sense and Quantic Dream is trying to break into it with a Magic the Gathering-esque spin on the format. Players build a deck of cards before queuing into teams of 3, then face off as battling mages, summoning creatures, building fortifications and casting spells rather than choosing a Hero with unique abilities in the traditional MOBA style.

Beta content includes a new map, 6 new spells and 5 new summon creatures for your deck, as well as 3 new buildings too.

Also new for this second closed beta is an introduction and tutorial for some of the game’s finer details, as well as a text chat for strategising and much-needed player reporting system to go with it. It will also feature early versions of the Spellcaster customisation system and ranked matches.

Spellcasters Chronicles is the first ever multiplayer online game from Quantic Dream, the French studio best known for cinematic narrative games like Detroit: Become Human, Heavy Rain and Beyond: Two Souls.

A TV adaptation of the latter game is reportedly in development, or the rights for one have been acquired at least. Elsewhere, Quantic Dream’s long-rumoured game in the Star Wars franchise was revealed as Star Wars Eclipse, a return-to-type narrative action game set in the High Republic era of a galaxy far, far away.

Don't despair though, below we've compiled a Top War tier list of all the best heroes in the game so you can choose the best ones according to your needs. The heroes can provide specific buffs and their kit can be extremely good in certain situations, but if you really want some additional info about these heroes, I've got you covered.

Most of the heroes on the Top War tier list are SSR Before we take a look at the Top War tier list though, I'll start by mentioning that the rarity of the heroes (SSR, SR, and R) plays a very important role in the game. The higher a hero's rarity, the more troops can join them in battle (SSR heroes can take a lot more troops than R heroes).

Therefore, it shouldn't come as a surprise that all the top-tier heroes are SSR. If you want to get SSR heroes too, all you need to do is keep playing the game - even as a f2p player you are bound to get a few eventually!

All the heroes have a type - some of them are Air Force heroes, some are Army heroes, and others are Navy Heroes. In the tier list, you will find them all divided by their type, so it will be a lot easier for you to pick the best ones based on what they should specialize in.

If you want to learn more about the game, make sure you check out our other Top War articles!

Maximo - A powerful hero that will greatly enhance any air force units and can quite literally change the entire course of a battle. He's a premium hero who is worth investing in, and by all means, one who can work on the offensive and defensive front.

Selina - She's a good hero thanks to the amazing buffs she provides, and if you manage to max her out, she greatly increases the maximum HP of other units, as well as their attack. Serval - Another broken premium hero that can make life a living hell for enemies. She's especially good when paired up with some of the other top-tier heroes, since they can stack their stats.

Preycis - This Army hero is great for aiming at the back-row enemies and is one of the best at specialising in that. He doesn't have a whole lot of other buffs (when compared to other heroes), but the sheer amount of damage dealt to the back row cannot go unnoticed. Shinji Ikari - A highly versatile hero, he can be obtained for a limited time only, but during that time, it's crucial to get him. He can be used for pretty much any type of content and has an ability that grants indestructibility for two rounds, which is definitely worth it. Optimus Prime - Another collab character that is impossible to overlook is Optimus Prime, the best Transformer out there (correct?). He can also grant an indestructibility buff, and when maxed out, is absolutely top-tier.

#4154. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Crowned 2026's "Best-Selling Physical Video Game In The US"

The Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2 got off to an outstanding start, selling over five million copies (approx 5.2 million units) in just four days. Sales in the UK and Japan have contributed to this, and now, Circana Retail Tracking Service has shared data about the title's US launch.

As highlighted by Circana's senior director and video game industry advisor Mat Piscatella (via social media), "after just one week", Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 is this year's "best-selling physical video game in the US". Interestingly, it's the first title to surpass one million physical units in a US launch week since the 2023 Switch title, The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Considering the year is almost over, and Grand Theft Auto 6's retail release is actually a "code-in-box", we imagine Ocarina's remake will hold onto the title of 2026's best-selling physical game (that's actually a proper physical game). However, there is one technicality - Circana tracks and reports "code-in-box" sales as "new physical video game sales", so Zelda may not actually keep the crown. And GTA 6 has already smashed pre-order records.

According to Nintendo's official data, Ocarina of Time is currently the second-highest selling Switch 2 game globally. As we previously noted, this puts it ahead of Donkey Kong Bananza's lifetime sales of 5.05 million, and the Switch 2 launch title Mario Kart World leads with 16.48 million sales. So it's still a tremendous effort for the remake of the legendary N64 title.

In our review here on Nintendo Life, we awarded Ocarina of Time's Switch 2 remake 9/10 stars, calling it the "best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time". After a brief dip to 95, it's once again sitting on a Metacritic score of 96/100.

#4153. Ocarina of Time Remake Actually Shows Its Entire Story Before Link's Adventure Begins

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

One of the best things about revisiting a game like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is discovering little details you might have missed the first time around. The remake has already given fans plenty of reasons to explore every corner of Hyrule again, but one particularly interesting discovery might have been hiding in plain sight from the very beginning.

When visiting Princess Zelda for the first time as Child Link, players can spot a tapestry inside one of the windows in Hyrule Castle's courtyard. And this tapestry actually depicts the entire story of the remake, including events that players are only supposed to see after completing the adventure.

Even stranger, this is the same tapestry that can be unlocked through the game's Threads of Time feature after finishing the main story. In other words, the game is showing you the full journey before Link even takes his first steps toward becoming the Hero of Time!

Link has always been known as the silent hero of Hyrule, but the remake appears to have given him a very brief spoken line.

You just need to move the camera in the right direction to catch it (thankfully, the remake's new dedicated camera controls make that little discovery much easier). Here, take a look for yourself: see the tapestry in the original Reddit post.

This discovery is particularly interesting when you consider what happened in the Nintendo 3DS version of Ocarina of Time. Back then, the same window featured a mural referencing The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword, serving both as a bit of cross-promotion and a way to connect the lore of the two games. The remake, however, has replaced that reference with something much more specific to the adventure we're playing.

When visiting Princess Zelda for the first time as Child Link, players can spot a tapestry inside one of the windows in Hyrule Castle's courtyard.

And naturally, fans haven't wasted any time coming up with explanations! One of the most popular theories suggests that the tapestry is further evidence that we're literally reliving the legend of the Hero of Time. After all, if the entire story is already depicted inside the castle, perhaps the events of Ocarina of Time are not simply unfolding for the first time. They're a story that Hyrule's people already know, one that keeps being told and experienced across generations.

Others have taken the discovery as a reason to look at the game's story from a different perspective. If the Royal Family knew what was coming, perhaps they also knew that Ganondorf would eventually be defeated by the Hero of Time. In that case, accepting the events as they were foretold might have seemed safer than trying to interfere with a fate they believed was already written.

Nintendo has expanded one of the original Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most heartbreaking side stories.

But that interpretation also raises an amusing question: why does Zelda still tell Link that her father doesn't believe Ganondorf is up to no good? I mean, he may not completely believe her, but the tapestry clearly shows the Gerudo king's eventual transformation into a monstrous beast and his attempt to kill both Link and Zelda! You'd think that would be enough to convince the king to be a little more suspicious.

Either way, we have another theory, which is probably the most creative and crazy one (so, naturally, also my personal favorite). Some players believe that the tapestry appears unusually far to the left inside the castle corridor, leaving what looks like plenty of empty wall space beside it. And if you've been following the community's ongoing hunt for clues about a potential Majora's Mask remake, you can probably guess where this is going!

Yes, some fans believe that the empty space is intentional, potentially leaving room for more tapestries depicting other legendary adventures. The next one could very well represent Majora's Mask, especially if Nintendo is planning another remake using the same approach as Ocarina of Time.

Of course, there's no confirmation that this is what Nintendo has in mind, and an empty wall is hardly definitive evidence of another Zelda remake. Still, I can't help but love the idea that this seemingly harmless decoration is actually a little tease of what's coming next!

#4152. The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Easter Eggs That Did And Did Not Make It Into The 2026 Remake

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is a game full of Easter Eggs, secrets, and hidden mechanics (did you know if a butterfly lands on your Deku Stick, it summons a fairy?). Now in its second remake, not every secret has made its way forward through the previous iterations, but many have. Below you will learn about a few of the secrets that made the cut, and others that didn’t.

In the courtyard where Link first meets Zelda, there is arguably the most fourth-wall-breaking Easter Egg in the whole game. If you don’t rush to Zelda and instead pause and enter first-person to look around, you will see portraits of other Nintendo characters through the windows, like Mario and Yoshi. In the 3DS remake, the portraits are replaced by an image of a Mario stage.

For the 2026 remake, there are no references to other Nintendo characters. Instead, the tapestry you build over the course of the game is on display. Removing the reference to Nintendo characters outside of the Zelda universe is understandable, but it is a little odd that art representing the full adventure of the game – an adventure that has not yet concluded – is on the wall.

As stated above, the Nintendo character portraits are gone, but there is still a guard you can annoy. If you fire a Deku Seed into the left window, a guard will pop out, yell at you, and then throw a bomb at you. You can’t pick up the bomb. In fact, at this point in the game, you haven’t even seen a bomb.

The Hyrule Castle portrait references to Yoshi and Mario are gone (though Mario and Luigi are still kind of in the game in a way), but Bowser gets a pass for some reason. Both Malon and her dad, Talon, are still wearing Bowser pins on their clothes. And unlike the N64 game where the detail was a little vague, there is no mistaking it here.

Gossip Stones are all over Ocarina of Time and it takes a while to understand what they do. If you hit them with a sword, they tell you the time, and if you play Zelda’s Lullaby near them, they refill your magic. If you do the Happy Mask Salesman’s side quest, interacting with them while wearing the Mask of Truth offers little hints and details about the world. But then there are interactions that are just odd for no reason. Blowing up a bomb near a Gossip Stone still makes it take off like a rocket ship, and using the Megaton Hammer still flattens them for a moment like a Looney Tunes.

And speaking of playing Zelda’s Lullaby for inanimate objects, if you slash a sign to pieces with your sword and regret your words and deeds, you can play the iconic tune to make the signs reform and become readable again.

This detail was exclusive to the 3DS remake of Ocarina of Time, and surprising no one, it has been removed. Ocarina of Time launched in June 2011 and Nintendo released Skyward Sword about five months later in November. For… marketing purposes, I guess, Skyward Sword art could be found in Lonlon Ranch, the Bombchu Shop in Hyrule Castle Town, and the Gerudo Fortress. It was a fun Easter Egg to discover back in 2011, especially since Skyward Sword was still months away, but these days it’s a bit of an odd inclusion.

Though never explicit, the composer ghosts guarding the Sun’s Song (and Link’s first ReDead encounter) have always been assumed to be inspired by Mario and Luigi. They are brothers; Flat is short, squat, and red; Sharp is lanky and green. They still appear in Ocarina of Time this way, which isn't surprising, since they are important characters you must meet to get a very useful song. Fans have also speculated that Talon and Ingo are Mario and Luigi-inspired for similar reasons, but it’s worth noting that they are not brothers.

In the Spirit Temple there is a large statue of a woman and for reasons that have never been explained, Link could attach his hookshot to her breasts. It served no purpose. It didn’t help solve a puzzle. If anything, it was confusing. But we all tried it and there is no shame in admitting it! That was removed for the 3DS remake, and it remains removed in 2026.

This is a very subtle reference to Wind Waker/Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom and is potentially the only addition to the remake that looks toward the future of the Zelda franchise. Obviously, plenty of characters in Ocarina later appear in Majora’s Mask (another remake of that is hopefully being considered), but it would be inaccurate to call those intentional Easter Eggs.

However, in Kokiri Forest and in the neighboring Lost Woods, the magical debris floating in the air often resembles a Korok as it would later appear in the series. It makes sense, too, because the Koroks are meant to be what the Kokiri transformed into following The Great Flood.

For more on the Ocarina of Time remake, you can find our review here. You can also find our interview with the game's producers here.

Chromatic Beings Everbright, the latest major Infinity Nikki update, has arrived, bringing Chinese New Year celebrations vibe to the game.

Infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, open-world dress-up RPG, has delivered yet another big content drop in the form of Chromatic Beings Everbright. The latest update brings the game up to version 2.2, and introduces a new narrative chapter, and gameplay taking place around a festival narrative.

If you couldn’t guess already, the new theme is Bloom Festival, inspired by Chinese New Year celebrations.

The big new story chapter takes place in the Infinity Nikki’s Wanxiang Realm. This deceptively serene and blissful region hides a dark secret, however. Chromafaces, the mythical inhabitants of the realm, have to embody fixed identities that dictate how they live and work.

These are doled out through Character Tokens, which are used to assign roles to each individual. The story follows Nikki as she uncovers the script that runs the realm and the facade it props up. Nikki will help free Chromafaces and dispel the illusion.

The Wanxiang Realm is split into three areas. Cai Ye is your typical lantern-lit district, where festivals and fireworks happen. Kongming Gorge is almost the opposite of that; a quiet and cold place. Finally, Jiuhua Pavilion literally floats above the region, and it's home to neverending music and dance.

The other big addition in 2.2 are the two new 5-Star Resonance Outfits with some interesting gameplay implications. Where Wanxiang Weaves Life is inspired by wuxia aesthetics, and true to its inspirations, it lets Nikki shapeshift into different Spirit Personas - and automatically collect resources in her vicinity.

Chroma's Mortal Heart, on the other hand, allows Nikki to fly around the Wanxiang Realm, drawing on the power of the Celestial Deer. This outfit also uses Celestial Deer Vision to automatically ping and mark treasure chests around her.

You can also look forward to Nefarious Shadows, a new Ability Outfit, which lets Nikki see through disguises, and reveals hidden paths in the world.

As with every major update, of course, there are themed activities and limited-time events throughout. Hotpot House is a cooking minigame where you attempt to run the eponymous restaurant, whereas Flavor Frenzy is series of platforming challenges that tasks you with gathering ingredients. Fortune Mahjong is a little more straightforward, with support for solo and multiplayer play.

#4149. Thrifty Business review - "The coziest management sim you'll ever play"

I never thought I'd come across something that manages to impress me to this extent - until Thrifty Business, at least. And let me tell you: I was beyond impressed. So, this is not just a simple Thrifty Business review; this is me telling you why you need to give it a try.

I play a lot of games. And by a lot, I mean A LOT. So, at this point, it takes quite a bit for something to genuinely surprise me.

I expected a cute little shop management sim (as per the Play Store images). Maybe something to play for a few hours and decorate a few shelves. Well, it didn't happen quite like that. I ended up spending far more time than I'd expected rearranging furniture and getting excited over witchy items.

In essence, you can buy unwanted items from NPCs in the form of mystery boxes. Then, you place them on the shelves and organise them by category. Later on, you can even organise events and expand. That's it.

Honestly, what's not to love? Grab your tea and blanket and get cosy - we'll talk gameplay! In terms of gameplay, you have all the freedom you need as a shopkeeper. You can genuinely make the place feel like your own. From finding the perfect spot for an item to rearranging displays, you're the boss.

You can even redecorate as much as you like - there's no restriction on that (thankfully), so in a way, you can play this in your own way. I mean, you can even skip decorating altogether and just play for the dialogue or for making money.

Personally, I'm always going to choose decorating over anything else, even at the cost of buying additional items.

On the topic of additional items, Thrifty Business doesn't try to turn running a shop into a stressful experience. There's no pressure to maximise every penny or deal with impatient customers.

Even if you end up making no sales in a day, the system still has a way to keep you progressing by offering a free mystery box every day. Not that they're particularly expensive (at the beginning, at least), but it's little details like this that make me appreciate the thought put into the experience.

Just a fair warning though: it's the kind of sim where you tell yourself "I'll play for another ten minutes", only to realise an entire hour flew by. The pixel graphics: love at first sight Can we please talk about the aesthetics?

The colourful 90s atmosphere makes the entire experience feel like a warm hug.

As someone who grew up during that time, seeing all those nostalgic items brought into 2026 put a smile on my face. I'd almost forgotten all about the Slinky!

Since I mentioned it, let me make one thing clear: there are a lot of items you can acquire in Thrifty Business. I mean A LOT. With so many of them, it's hard not to appreciate the sheer amount of work that must have gone into designing all those individual sprites. Not everyone's cup of tea - but maybe everyone's cup of hot cocoa? I have to admit, Thrifty Business understands exactly what kind of experience it wants to offer. It's not one of those fast-paced tycoons where you rush to make millions from the get-go.

That might not make it into everyone's favourite list, but it is bound to make it into some. If you're over here reading this and you have someone special in your life who likes Stardew Valley, then Thrifty Business is something you can definitely surprise them with.

Really, sometimes, all you need is to escape into a cute little world, put things on shelves, decorate to your heart's content, and call it a day. Life is too fast-paced sometimes anyway, and Thrifty Business can be the escape that is one tap away. You need to play with the sound on The audio deserves some love too, and I believe Spellgarden Games did an amazing job creating a soundtrack that perfectly complements the sim. I honestly couldn't fault it at all, and I'm usually the type to turn the sound off after spending more than five hours with a game. Not this time, though...

An ode to the queer community As if the cosy atmosphere wasn't enough, I absolutely adore the queer representation woven into this.

From the story (which you should absolutely read - I won't give you any spoilers) to the item categories and even character creation, there's something about the sense of community you get in this little virtual world that gives you a fuzzy feeling inside. Not too many games celebrate individuality, self-expression, and simply being yourself in a way that feels "just right".

Now, if you'll excuse me, I have a shop to rearrange. Again.

#4148. Civilization Studio Fires a Third of Staff, Including Its Lead

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Certain developers focusing on specific genres is nothing new, especially when they helped define how those genres are perceived in the modern day. While it does wonders to ensure the team is working within their skill set, it can also come back to bite if the genre in question is on the niche side, relying on a smaller fanbase to keep up with constantly rising quality goals.

Arion Kurtaj has pleaded guilty to the 2022 Rockstar Games hack that leaked Grand Theft Auto 6 footage and source code.

In a shocking turn, Firaxis, the team behind massive hits like XCOM and Civilization, has been gutted with the owning company, Take-Two, laying off a whopping third of the studio. With 60 major players ousted, including the head of the studio, the surviving team has been left reeling, still working on long-awaited titles that had yet to turn around.

Firaxis is a very specialized team, working entirely on their series XCOM and Civilization to deliver different kinds of large-scale tactics gameplay to millions across the decades. Now, right after the middling release of Civilization 7 and years into the newest entry in XCOM, losing members is the exact opposite of what the team needs.

Despite this, a spokesperson for Take-Two, Firaxis’ parent company, described it as “restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength.” The shrinking team is meant to allow them to operate faster, with a bit of a sleeker ship doctrine to keep things tight as they continue development.

Even so, the team is clearly going to see some major hiccups both in morale and speed, right as the current XCOM project had “...faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone over the summer.” Without major senior staff in the picture, especially the loss of studio head Heather Hazen, I can’t imagine they’ll suddenly be able to hit the ground running.

Firaxis had suffered layoffs as recently as this last September, making this new blow almost feel like a punishment for Civilization 7’s mixed reception. The studio has really struggled to keep up with the constant graphical pushes set by the rest of the industry, with many of their most recent titles suffering from frame issues and performance stutters.

Certain developers focusing on specific genres is nothing new, especially when they helped define how those genres are perceived in the modern day.

Even with their recent hiccups, Firaxis is an absolute titan of strategy gaming, and seeing them continue to spiral is a major blow to the industry. Especially following Take-Two’s major financial win through GTA 6 preorders and the absolute truckload they’re about to make off of the game’s full release, it feels like Firaxis doesn’t need to be hung over the fire like this.

Firaxis is truly one of the original greats, boasting over 30 years of history and genre-defining development that has established what people want from both civilization-building and squad-based tactics. For what it's worth, Firaxis’s mixed launch of Civilization 7 is a major speed bump they needed to be a win.

Their work is some of the most important in the space, bringing tactics titles to millions who wouldn’t have otherwise touched them, giving them an in on a niche but thriving genre that needs the players now more than ever. It feels like the long dev times that have plagued Firaxis have let indie teams and more specialized titles steal their lunch, leaving them out to dry.

It’s hard to say, because performance definitely matters in the gaming industry’s job paths, but this most recent massive cutdown feels shortsighted, to say the least. How is a team that is already struggling to complete a title supposed to speed up after a 33% staff cut, after all? Take-Two has more than enough breathing room, and it feels like they might be getting a little greedy as Grand Theft Auto 6 approaches.

Limbus's Season 8 is well on its way, and we finally have an idea of what's happening when coming into the new year.

#4147. The Switch 2 Pro Controller Can Make Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Even Better

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time hit Switch 2 today, and, as Kyle Hilliard pointed out in our review, it is pretty excellent. Along with its remarkable visual upgrade, the new Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time adds quality-of-life improvements and modernizes the control scheme. As part of that, Nintendo has added the ability to jump and sprint. While that works well to make the game feel new, I quickly realized it sometimes clashes with another new improvement: a free camera controlled by the right stick. Holding down the sprint button to get through areas as fast as possible can make it tricky to keep the camera where you want it, but thankfully, if you have the Switch 2 Pro Controller, there's an easy fix.

After hours of running around, I was awestruck by the level of detail and updates, but I found myself constantly fighting with the camera, or at the very least, needing to take a strange claw-style grip to be able to direct the camera with the right stick, while holding down the A button to sprint. If you're a casual Switch 2 player, you might not have even noticed the back buttons on the Pro Controller, or you just have no idea what they do. Those buttons can be remapped on a per-game basis and it's a simple process. Everyone has their own preferences, but, for example, for high-mobility shooters, I like remapping one of those to reload and one to jump. I've never felt the need to remap in a Zelda game, but after feeling the need to do so with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, I might do so going forward.

If you, like me, struggle to comfortably steer the new free camera while running through hallways, towns, dungeons, and, yes, Hyrule Field, you might want to consider remapping your controller. As you can see in the above image, the placement of Jump and Dash on the face buttons can make it difficult to simultaneously control the camera and sprint. This isn't typically a problem in most modern games, as clicking the right stick is often a toggle to sprint, but in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, you need to hold the button.

If you have the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller, copying one button's functionality to the buttons on the back of the controller is simple. All you need to do is hold the Home button on the Switch 2 Pro Controller for a moment until the Switch 2 system menu appears on the right side. Along with Power Options and any Bluetooth audio devices you have available, there is also the option to map GL and GR, the controller's back buttons on the left and right, respectively.

Navigate down the menu to the GL and GR, then select which one you'd like to map. It will ask you which button you want to assign to the one you selected. Everyone can choose whatever makes sense in their own head, but mapping A (Roll and Dash) to GL and X (Jump) to GR made the most sense to me. Now, while I'm using the Switch 2 Pro Controller, I can use my middle finger to hold the GL button to Dash around without removing my thumb from the camera-controlling right stick.

And the best part is that, since you're not removing the functionality of the A or X buttons, you can still use them when it makes sense. For example, A also controls actions like opening up a treasure chest or door, and in my head, that feels like a face-button action, whereas rolling and dashing feel right mapped to the back buttons. The only downside is that, since this functionality is new for Switch 2 Pro Controllers, it isn't available if you're using the Joy-Cons or a Switch 1 Pro Controller. Also, it can make switching over to handheld mode challenging, as you don't have access to the back buttons in that play style.

Even if you don't have the ability to take advantage of this tip, either because you don't own a Switch 2 Pro Controller or because you prefer playing in handheld mode, you should still absolutely play the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. To learn more about the experience and why it's a must-play, head to our review.

#4146. Path to Nowhere tier list - All characters ranked

Updated on November 2nd, 2026 - Version: 1.9.54

Path to Nowhere has a considerable variety of characters you can unlock. But if you are a beginner, finding out what hero to use can be problematic. Luckily, experts across the web have created a tier list for Path to Nowhere to solve this problem.

We have similar articles like this Neural Cloud tier list and Summoners War: Chronicles tier list, where we have also ranked all of the characters by their power and abilities from the best to worst. If you're playing different mobile games, try to search around - our website is brimming with tier lists and various guides for the most popular games. WHAT IS THE PATH TO NOWHERE TIER LIST?

This Path to Nowhere tier list is similar to the ones we have for other video games. There are four tiers: S, A, B, and C. Continue reading, and you will learn more about every tier.

Most players consider Demon to be the most overpowered hero in the game. His special attack stacks a shield for him and his allies. The more health points Demon has, the more powerful protection he will create.

He also has potent attack stats, allowing him to kill enemies fast.

Nox is the most accessible hero in Tier S. She can be unlocked by completing the 14-day event. Nox has incredibly high DPS and a passive ability that decreases your enemies’ defence. Moreover, Nox increases attack points upon killing enemies, which is one of the best abilities in Path to Nowhere. So, make sure to obtain this hero as soon as you can.

Labyrinth is the only hero in Tier S that has a B rarity. So, you can unlock her even if you don't play the game daily. Labyrinth is a damage dealer who takes the primary role in a team. She can break enemies’ shields and even destroy Demon’s shield.

Even though Baiyi has less DPS than Nox, she still can deal a lot of damage in a short period. Moreover, her skill significantly increases critical rate boost. She is also one of the fastest heroes in Path to Nowhere.

Langley is a top-level hero because of her particular skill. It provides you with an AoE attack that can hit a 3x3 area. So, Langley is a perfect option if you want to fight against bosses or groups of enemies.

Eirene is a magical attacker that probably has one of the best passive abilities in the game. While using an auto-attack, she creates a black hole that hits a 3x3 area. The only disadvantage is that Eirene is weak in melee fights.

Hamel is the only healer in Path to Nowhere that is worth being in Tier S. She has an AoE healing effect that helps keep your team's HP topped up in battle.

Countless Chelsea is one of the most complex heroes in Path to Nowhere. But in good hands, she brings excellent results. Countless Chelsea can summon a panther that can be used as a shield. Also, she has damage reduction, allowing her to take a lot of punishment and still survive.

The main feature of Demolia is her health points. She can quickly increase them and, after that, heal herself, which significantly increases her survivability. The only reason why she's not in Tier S is that there is a limit on her HP boost and healing.

Even though Serpent looks cute, she is one of the deadliest heroes in Path to Nowhere. While using a standard attack, she applies a slowdown effect to enemies and increases her speed. Moreover, when there are no enemies near Serpent, she will raise her attack.

RouLecca has poor DPS and can only deal damage using critical attacks, but she can increase her crit rate and damage while attacking.

Zoya is the Tier A hero most likely to appear in Tier S in the future. She has a 3x3 AoE attack that can deal significant damage. Zoya also has a lot of health points and has no problem killing enemies in short range. But the best thing about Zoya is her passive skill. It increases her attacking speed, making her suitable even in the later stages of the game.

Pricilla can summon a clone who helps her during battle. Additionally, she has high DPS, allowing you to kill enemies quickly. Unfortunately, her lack of health points doesn't make her worthy of becoming Tier S.

Hecate's ability has long range and hits every target in this range, which is extremely powerful. But Hecate doesn't have good survivability, so you should be careful while using her.

Aerial is the only healer in Tier A. The only difference between her and Hamel is that she is universal. Aerial has increased damage, which enables her to fight against enemies. And for increased damage, she gives up her healing capabilities. So, Aerial can't heal as effectively as Hamel.

Victoria is a hero with really significant damage. However, she forgoes health points for such a high attack capability. She will lower her health points to gain more attacks and kill enemies more effectively.

Luvia Ray is the most classic damage dealer in Path to Nowhere. She has high stats and a passive skill oriented toward increasing attack. Overall, she is a mighty hero who will always bring benefit to your team.

Crache has one of the best special attacks in the game. The AoE can deal a high amount of damage quickly. Moreover, this attack has an unblocking effect, so that opponents can't dodge it. The only disadvantage of Crache is that she has purely physical stats. Therefore, she must be complemented by powerful characters who can deal a lot of damage.

The best thing about EMP is that this hero is free. You can obtain her by completing the first chapter of the story. As for battle, she is perfectly suitable for the role of a background hero. Her special attack can wipe out low HP heroes and provide additional buffs for your team.

Tier B includes the following characters:

You can find out more about the most powerful heroes from Tier B below.

Cinnabar is a unique combination of powerful abilities in one character. She can create a 3x3 range shield protecting allies. Even though this shield doesn't have many health points, using it can still be handy during battles. Overall, Cinnabar is pretty powerful. She has a strong multiplier, allowing her to win battles easily.

Ninety-Nine is one of the best tanks in Path to Nowhere. You can exchange her health points in order to deal damage to enemies. On top of that, her extraordinary ability will reduce her health to get a significant attack bonus.

Sumire hits four times in a row in the same direction with her Special Ability. This special is extremely powerful on small maps, making Sumire more effective there. Also, she increases her damage when someone is opposite to her. Moreover, there are no limitations on increasing damage.

Even though Wolverine can't play the central role in the team, his slowing-down effect allows him to be effective even with higher-tier characters. Wolverine has special traps that stun enemies. These traps have a high range, making this hero super helpful.

Tier C includes characters that aren't recommended to use, even if you are a beginner.

The main feature of Pepper is her powerful attack speed. She can even increase it using a particular skill. But the main problem with Pepper is that she has no other stats to boast about.

There is nothing special about Gekkabijin. She has no powerful stats like the Tier S characters. Her unique ability provides her with additional attack and shield, but it isn't good enough to be competitive nowadays.

Even though the game has different characters with distinct abilities, it's best to only use the ones at the top of our Path to Nowhere tier list if you can - Tier S and Tier A - since they consistently perform the best.

Thank you for reading this guide - hope you find it helpful! And while you are here, make sure to read our Path to Nowhere beginner's guide as well.

Belmont's Curse is currently available for the Switch. While there's no Switch 2 Edition, if you do play this title on Nintendo's new hardware, you'll get a frame rate boost. And if you haven't tried it out yet, you can download a demo from the eShop.

You can find out more about this new Castlevania entry iun our review here on Nintendo Life. We gave it 8/10 stars, calling it "one of the best Castlevania games in a long time thanks to its combat variety and smart whip integrations".

#4143. The Pocket Gamer Podcast Episode 103 - The Pocket Gamer Awards voting phase is now open! And, inevitably, Warhammer Survivors

What makes a franchise adaptation successful for you? And who do you think will win in a popularity contest: Dadish, Zayne, or GingerBrave? We dive into all things Warhammer Survivors in this week's (New and Improved!) Pocket Gamer Podcast, with a healthy dose of speculation on the community-nominated characters from the Pocket Gamer Awards in the mix.

The results for the nominations phase are in, and for Best Mobile Game Character, I'm surprised to see Zayne in there as opposed to Valko from Love and Deepspace! It's a pleasant surprise, of course, as I've always liked Zayne, while Iwan shares his thoughts on controversies and white bread.

Will believes that Dadish deserves the top spot, and it's up to you, the community, to pick your winners as voting is now open until the end of the year. Hopefully, you'll get to see your faves win at the awards show in London in January!

That said, we move on from the nomms onto Warhammer Survivors, which is the hot topic for the three of us in particular this week - and that's because we are all playing on different platforms, coming from different perspectives, and have mixed opinions on the Survivors-like.

For me, as a newbie to the franchise, the Warhammer coat of paint isn't really relevant to me, but even so, I had a blast playing through the roguelike as it is. I love the challenge and the replayability, as well as the lovely little surprises you get to unlock along the way. Iwan, on the other hand, feels like while it's a worthy entry into the genre, it lacks that extra spark that made the original Vampire Survivors so great.

Will is a bit of both - he thinks it's not the perfect game, but it's got enough going for it that makes it charming in its own way, especially for a Warhammer fan. With the roadmap for the roguelike having just been revealed, here's hoping we'll get to see more updates for it to make it shine like it should in the next few weeks!

You can listen to the podcast below, through the Spotify embed, or head over to our Spotify Page. If you fancy giving us a follow, you'll actually get the new podcasts pushed to you as they're uploaded (which means you can give them a listen before we've even got the story live on the website).

Plus, we've been teasing more ways of getting it to you for the past months, and now the time has finally come. You can catch us on Amazon Music or on Apple Podcasts too - because life is hard enough already, and we wouldn't want you to struggle with finding us!

#4142. Starsand Island is a life and farming sim that isn't gacha, and it's out next week

Starsand Island officially has an Early Access release date, and it sounds like it won't stay there for years.

Though it may seem like we just had a big life sim release in Heartopia, 2026 actually has more than one highly-anticipated release in that particular subgenre of cozy game. The next big one on the horizon is Starsand Island, the life and farming sim from Seed Sparkle Lab.

The game has been gaining momentum since the launch of a demo in October last year, but the developer never quite managed to commit to a date for its debut title. Until now.

Seed Sparkle Lab announced today that Starsand Island will enter Early Access on February 11, which is only a bit over one week from now. This goes for Steam and the Xbox Preview Program version.

The developer said to expect a fairly short Early Access run, as the full launch is expected in the summer of this year. When the full release arrives, the game will also make the jump to PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series, as well as Switch 2.

The full release is also expected to bring Steam Deck support and introduce the multiplayer mode, which will not be available during Early Access

Starsand Island has something of a unique look compared to other games in the subgenre. The storybook, anime-inspired aesthetics are popular in the realm of gacha games, of course. However, seeing as this particular game isn’t gacha, being a premium product means it’s going to offer something free-to-play games aren’t designed to.

Speaking of which, the game will be available in two editions: Standard and Deluxe, with the latter including Romanticism-inspired outfits, furniture, and other customisation items. If you buy either during launch, you’ll also get a Chinese New Year bonus with even more outfits and furniture.

On top of the usual systems of farming, mining, and making friends with adorable characters (and animals), the game also has combat that pits you against ancient guardians. You can, of course, also build a home in it, and decorate it to your heart's content.

Seed Sparkle Lab says you can expect about 100 hours of content in the Early Access launch build, and more features will arrive over the course of the next six or so months, including a crossover event with My Time At Portia.

You can look forward to more Starsand Island coverage from us in the near future. Until then, you can get started by planning who you’re going to date now.

#4140. Cozy Tanuki Adventure Dev Explains Why It Launched Between Zelda And GTA 6

Most studios wouldn't pick the week between The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and GTA 6 to launch their debut game, but Denkiworks did. Its cozy adventure, Tanuki: Pon's Summer, arrived on November 10, and the three-person studio says there were good reasons to take the risk.

Discover the official release date and survival mechanics of Wilderdark from the creators of Monstrum.

The Kyoto studio's debut follows Pon, a tanuki delivering packages by BMX while restoring a shrine before a summer festival. It's a very different game from Rockstar's crime epic, but that doesn't make finding an audience in November any easier.

In an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, Denkiworks co-founder and game director Liam Edwards explained why the team stuck with November and what it hopes happens once players have had their fill of the bigger games.

The date wasn't chosen to challenge Nintendo or Rockstar. Denkiworks first aimed for summer but needed longer to finish the game and prepare a multiplatform release. October became the next target, until platform marketing opportunities made November more attractive, Edwards explained.

Less competition doesn't always mean better visibility for a small studio. Denkiworks also secured a publishing deal with Critical Reflex and an early agreement to bring Tanuki: Pon's Summer to Xbox Game Pass. Both offered ways to reach players beyond what the studio could manage alone.

There was another practical hurdle. Denkiworks wanted the game available across PC and consoles at launch, which is a lot to ask of a three-person core team. With help from its publisher, an external porting team handled the Xbox, original Switch, and PlayStation versions, while Denkiworks concentrated on PC and Switch 2. Launching everywhere took coordination, but it also meant players wouldn't have to wait for their preferred platform.

Then came the surprise. Nintendo released its Ocarina of Time remake on November 5, just five days before Tanuki: Pon's Summer. Edwards says the studio couldn't have anticipated the move. That left Tanuki squeezed between Nintendo's game and GTA 6, which launches November 19.

That may be the more awkward overlap. Edwards believes the audience for Pon's laid-back Japanese adventure is more likely to intersect with Zelda players than with people counting down the days to GTA 6. And Ocarina of Time's enormous opening shows just how much attention Nintendo's game has commanded. Trying to compete for the same players in the same week isn't an enviable position for a studio of this size.

Still, it's worth separating the unexpected Zelda release from the studio's own decision. Denkiworks chose November for the opportunities it offered. It didn't knowingly set out to challenge both giants, and Edwards isn't pretending the team can match their marketing budgets.

Rather than trying to win launch week, Edwards hopes Tanuki: Pon's Summer can stick around in people's minds. He described the game as a "lovely little underdog" and suggested that word of mouth could help it find an audience after players have moved on from Zelda and GTA 6. That's a different kind of release strategy from trying to dominate the charts on day one.

Denkiworks is betting that Pon's charm will do some of the work. Alongside delivering mail and performing BMX tricks, players can get to know the island's residents, take part in activities, and rebuild the Great Tanuki Shrine. With so many major releases competing for attention, Pon's laid-back adventure offers something quite different.

For Denkiworks, the goal isn't to beat Zelda or GTA 6. It's to make a game people remember when they're ready to play something else.

For Denkiworks, the goal isn't to beat Zelda or GTA 6. It's to make a game people remember when they're ready to play something else.

That approach isn't risk-free. Launching next to two huge games could bury Tanuki before enough people notice it, and word of mouth isn't guaranteed. But Denkiworks has decided that useful platform support beats waiting endlessly for a perfect date.

#4139. Nioh 3 launches, immediately becomes the most played Nioh ever on Steam

Just a few hours after launch, Nioh 3 is already the biggest release in series history on Steam.

It sounds like Koei Tecmo’s decision to finally release a Nioh game on PC day-and-date with PlayStation has paid off. The highly-anticipated Nioh 3 has gone live across both platforms, a first for a series that typically spends its initial release months as a console exclusive.

On Steam, and despite having only been available for just a few hours, the game has broken series records, and it continues to climb.

At the time of writing, Nioh 3 has peaked at 42,822 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), and the number keeps going up. Because it’s in the middle of day in Europe and everyone is at work, it’s entirely possible - if not likely - that this figure will get much higher. A weekend bump is also possible, as we’ve seen with several recent releases.

As it stands, the current peak concurrent is enough to get the game in Steam’s top 20 most played games.

This already puts it ahead of all other Nioh games on Steam. The original Nioh peaked at 10,649 when it released in November, 2017. Nioh 2 fared much better, peaking at 41,325 concurrent players in February, 2021.

Of course, you could see that success coming a mile away. The game is currently number one worldwide in Steam’s list of top sellers. This is a jump of 46 positions, for a total of three weeks Nioh 3 has spent in that list.

There are many reasons as to why Nioh 3 has done as well as it has. Word of mouth coming off last year’s PS5-exclusive demo, and the more positive coverage that followed since are just two.

Just last week, Team Ninja released a pretty generous demo across both platforms, which has been well received by players, and likely contributed to sales, in no small part because progress in the demo carries over to the full game.

Critical reviews have been incredibly positive, too. We awarded the game four out of five stars, calling it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.” It will be interesting to see what number the highest peak concurrent actually settles on over the weekend.

Until then, if you’re jumping in yourself, our Nioh 3 guides are essential reading. Start off with these useful and actually informative gameplay tips, and don’t start playing until you’ve changed these settings. Once you’re ready to get deeper, be sure to read up on how to play co-op with other players, and how to summon AI Acolytes to help you out.

#4138. Pokémon Masters EX tier list - The best sync pairs to use

Updated on November 3rd, 2026 - Version:  2.74.0 - Latest Additions:  Arc Suit Hau & Raichu, Arc Suit Gladion & Silvally, Maxie (Fall 2026) & Ting-Lu

With over 200 collectable Sync Pairs of Pokémon and their masters, it sure can get confusing for new players and veterans alike to come to a definitive conclusion about which ones are the best and which ones they should avoid. Pokémon Masters EX, the officially licensed game by DeNA, has brought tons of new Sync Pairs for players to collect and use with their fifth anniversary. This Pokémon Masters EX tier list is here to serve as a curated list of Sync Pairs that can help you in your journey of becoming the best Pokémon trainer.

You will find all the answers in this tier list as to whether a certain Sync Pair is better or worse than another. Keep in mind that tier lists are inherently subjective in nature. Use your own judgment while investing your resources in these Sync Pairs, but feel free to take inspiration from them.

Stay tuned for the updated versions of this tier list - we will make sure to add new Sync Pairs as they are released while also adjusting the individual categories based on future balance adjustments.

Let’s get you right to our Pokémon Masters EX tier list!

The main focus of judging Sync Pairs in this tier list will be mostly on their damage-dealing capabilities. Most of the Sync Pairs here have striking abilities that help them deal more damage. Of course, some exceptions exist, like the Steven & Deoxys (Attack Forme) Sync Pair that can also boost the critical hit rate of all allies. However, that's just an added bonus to their already high damage multipliers and potential value.

Some of the most notable damage dealers are going to be Red & Pikachu, Lucas & Dialga, and Steven & Deoxys (Attack Forme). Red & Pikachu's special move B Thunderbolt is a massive hyper-scaling damaging move that increases its own damage the more it is used. Such moves are not only good in PvE content where fights can drag out, but also in certain PvP situations against tanky stall team comps. Lucas & Dialga is possibly the best Dragon-type Sync Pair available due to their special move Dragon Zone that can boost the stats of all Dragon-types. Steven & Deoxys (Attack Forme) is the ultimate counter to Sync Pairs that reduce the stats of enemies. Their passive ability, Downside Up, states that whenever an enemy reduces the stats of Steven and Deoxys (Attack Forme), the move instead increases their stats by the same amount.
